questions.stem: A 65-years-old patient presented to the emergency with high grade fever, chest pain, increased respiratory rate and cough with expectoration. His sputum was sent to the laboratory for gram straining which showed the presence of pus cells and gram-positive cocci in pair. Which of the following will help in confirming the diagnosis?
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. C) Bile solubility

 

The clinical presentation, including high-grade fever, chest pain, and increased respiratory rate, along with the Gram-stained finding of gram-positive cocci in pairs, points towards Streptococcus pneumoniae as the most likely causative agent. Streptococcus pneumoniae is distinct from other bacteria due to its arrangement in pairs (diplococci) and its characteristic alpha-hemolytic colonies on blood agar.

 

 

To confirm this diagnosis, the bile solubility test is performed. In this test, bile salts (such as sodium deoxycholate) are added to the culture, and Streptococcus pneumoniae colonies dissolve in the presence of bile, confirming the diagnosis. No other bacteria show this bile solubility.

 

Confirmatory tests for Streptococcus pneumoniae:

 

1. Bile solubility: Colonies dissolve in bile on blood agar.

 

 

2. Optochin sensitivity: Growth inhibited near an optochin-impregnated disk.

 

 

3. Inulin fermentation: Ability to ferment inulin, a specific sugar.

 

 

 Mnemonic: B-O-I (Bank of India)

 

  • B: Bile solubility
  • O: Optochin sensitivity
  • I: Inulin fermentation

 

Note:

 

 

 

 

 

Other Options:

 

Option A. Bacitracin sensitivity: This test is used to differentiate Group A Streptococcus (Streptococcus pyogenes) from other beta-hemolytic streptococci. Streptococcus pneumoniae is alpha-hemolytic and not identified using bacitracin sensitivity.

 

Option B. Catalase test: The catalase test differentiates between Staphylococcus (catalase-positive) and Streptococcus (catalase-negative). While Streptococcus pneumoniae is catalase-negative, this test alone is insufficient for confirming the specific diagnosis of pneumococcus.

 

Option D. Coagulase test: The coagulase test is used to distinguish Staphylococcus aureus (coagulase-positive) from other staphylococcal species. This test is unrelated to Streptococcus pneumoniae identification.

 

Educational Objective:

 

The bile solubility test is a key diagnostic tool for confirming Streptococcus pneumoniae, distinguishing it from other bacteria due to its unique colony dissolution in bile.

questions.stem: 2. A 40-year-old man underwent kidney transplantation. Two months after transplantation, he developed fever and feature suggestive of bilateral diffuse interstitial pneumonitis. Which of the following is most likely etiologic agent?
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. B) Cytomegalovirus

 

The patient’s presentation of bilateral diffuse interstitial pneumonitis post-transplantation strongly suggests cytomegalovirus (CMV) infection. CMV is a DNA virus belonging to the herpesvirus family and is a common opportunistic infection in immunocompromised individuals, particularly those undergoing organ transplantation. Post-transplant patients receive immunosuppressive therapy to prevent graft rejection, making them highly susceptible to infections.

 

CMV infection typically manifests within the first 6 months after transplantation. Pulmonary involvement leads to pneumonitis, which is a hallmark of CMV in transplant recipients.

 

Other Options:

 

Option A. Herpes simplex virus (HSV): HSV infections in immunocompromised individuals typically present as mucocutaneous lesions rather than pneumonitis. HSV is not a common cause of post-transplant pneumonia.

 

Option C. Epstein-Barr virus (EBV): EBV can cause post-transplant lymphoproliferative disorder (PTLD) but is not a typical cause of interstitial pneumonitis. PTLD usually involves lymphoid tissue, not the lungs.

 

Option D. Varicella-Zoster virus (VZV): VZV primarily causes skin-related conditions like shingles and, in rare cases, disseminated disease with pulmonary involvement, but it is not the most common cause of pneumonitis post-transplant.

 

Educational Objective:

 

Cytomegalovirus (CMV) is the most common viral cause of pneumonitis in post-transplant patients due to their immunocompromised status. 

 

Other common CMV-associated conditions include:

 

  • Congenital CMV (e.g., microencephaly, hepatosplenomegaly, skin rash)
  • Mononucleosis-like syndrome in immunocompetent individuals (simple tonsillitis)
  • Chorioretinitis in AIDS patients
  • Pneumonitis in transplant recipients.

questions.stem: With which of the following of viral hepatitis infection in pregnancy, the maternal mortality is highest:
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. D) Hepatitis E

 

Hepatitis E virus (HEV) is an RNA virus that belongs to the Hepeviridae family and is transmitted through the fecal-oral route, often due to contaminated water or food. HEV infection is generally self-limiting; however, in pregnant women, especially in the third trimester, it can lead to fulminant hepatitis (acute liver failure) with a significantly high risk of maternal mortality. The mortality rate can reach as high as 15-25% in this population.

 

In contrast, hepatitis A, B, and C infections are not associated with such a dramatic increase in maternal mortality during pregnancy. Hepatitis E infection in pregnancy presents with acute jaundice, increased liver enzyme levels, and a rapid decline in liver function, often necessitating urgent medical intervention.

 

Other Options:

 

Option A. Hepatitis A: Hepatitis A is an RNA virus from the Picornaviridae family and is transmitted via the fecal-oral route. It typically causes self-limited acute hepatitis and is not associated with chronic disease or increased mortality in pregnancy.

 

Option B. Hepatitis B: Hepatitis B is a DNA virus from the Hepadnaviridae family and is transmitted via parenteral, sexual, and vertical routes. Chronic infection with hepatitis B can lead to cirrhosis and hepatocellular carcinoma, but it is not associated with increased maternal mortality during acute infection in pregnancy.

 

Option C. Hepatitis C: Hepatitis C is an RNA virus from the Flaviviridae family, transmitted via parenteral, sexual, and vertical routes. Chronic hepatitis C can cause liver cirrhosis and hepatocellular carcinoma over time, but acute infection during pregnancy does not typically result in high maternal mortality.

 

Note:

 

 

Educational Objective:

 

Hepatitis E is the most common cause of fulminant hepatitis in pregnant women and is associated with a high maternal mortality rate, particularly in the third trimester. It is crucial to prevent HEV infections by maintaining proper sanitation and avoiding contaminated water and food sources.

questions.stem: True about Botulinum toxin:
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. B) Interfere with Cholinergic transmission

 

Botulinum toxin, produced by Clostridium botulinum, is a neurotoxin that blocks the release of acetylcholine at the neuromuscular junction, thereby interfering with cholinergic transmission. Acetylcholine is the primary neurotransmitter responsible for muscle contraction. The toxin acts by cleaving SNARE proteins (such as SNAP-25), which are necessary for the docking and release of synaptic vesicles containing acetylcholine. As a result, there is a lack of muscle contraction, leading to flaccid paralysis.

 

 

 

The clinical condition associated with this mechanism is known as floppy baby syndrome when occurring in infants and botulism in adults. Botulism can occur due to contaminated food or wound infections.

 

Note:

 

Spastic Paralysis: Caused by unopposed contraction due to inhibition of GABA and Glycine (seen in Tetanus).

 

  • First muscle affected: Masseter muscle (Lockjaw/Trismus).
  • Advanced stage: Opisthotonus (back muscles in full contraction, body forms a bow shape).

 

 

Other Options:

 

Option A. Interfere with adrenergic transmission: This is incorrect as adrenergic transmission involves neurotransmitters like norepinephrine and epinephrine, which are not directly affected by botulinum toxin.

 

Option C. Increase release of synaptic vesicles: This is incorrect as botulinum toxin prevents the release of synaptic vesicles containing acetylcholine, leading to reduced neurotransmitter availability rather than an increase.

 

Option D. Acts also on CNS: This is incorrect as botulinum toxin primarily acts at the peripheral neuromuscular junctions and does not cross the blood-brain barrier to affect the central nervous system (CNS).

 

Educational Objective:

 

Botulinum toxin inhibits cholinergic transmission by blocking acetylcholine release, leading to flaccid paralysis. It is used clinically in small doses for conditions such as muscle spasticity, dystonia, and cosmetic procedures to reduce wrinkles.

questions.stem: A patient is suffering from painful vesicular eruption at T-4 dermatome. The cause is:
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. B) Herpes zoster

 

The clinical presentation of a painful vesicular rash localized to a specific dermatome (T4) strongly indicates Herpes zoster infection. Herpes zoster, also known as shingles, is caused by the Varicella-zoster virus (VZV), which is the same virus responsible for chickenpox (primary infection). After the initial infection, VZV remains dormant in sensory ganglia and can reactivate later in life, particularly when the individual is immunocompromised or older.

 

Upon reactivation, the virus travels along the affected sensory nerve, causing a unilateral vesicular rash limited to the dermatome innervated by that nerve. The rash is usually associated with intense pain and burning, known as postherpetic neuralgia if the pain persists after the rash resolves.

 

 

Herpes Virus Family: DNA viruses with 8 types.

 

  • Type 1: Herpes Simplex Virus 1 (HSV-1)
  • Type 2: Herpes Simplex Virus 2 (HSV-2)
  • Type 3: Varicella Zoster Virus (VZV)
  • Type 4: Epstein-Barr Virus (EBV)
  • Type 5: Cytomegalovirus (CMV)
  • Types 6, 7, 8: Other lesser-known human herpesviruses.

 

Nerve-related complications of zoster:

 

  • Ophthalmic Zoster: Involvement of the third cranial nerve leading to vesicular rash in the eye, potentially causing blindness.
  • Ramsay-Hunt Syndrome: Involvement of the seventh cranial nerve causing facial palsy.

 

Other Options:

 

Option A. EBV infection: Epstein-Barr Virus (EBV) causes infectious mononucleosis and is not associated with dermatome-specific vesicular eruptions.

 

Option C. CMV infection: Cytomegalovirus (CMV) typically presents with systemic symptoms in immunocompromised patients, such as pneumonia or retinitis, rather than localized vesicular rashes.

 

Option D. Herpes simplex: Herpes simplex virus (HSV) can cause painful vesicular lesions, but these are typically localized to mucocutaneous areas such as the lips (HSV-1) or genital areas (HSV-2). HSV does not follow a dermatomal pattern.

 

Educational Objective:

 

Herpes zoster (shingles) is characterized by a unilateral, painful, vesicular rash following a specific dermatome due to the reactivation of latent Varicella-zoster virus (VZV). The T4 dermatome involvement indicates reactivation along the corresponding nerve. Remember that the rash never crosses the midline and often resolves with antiviral treatment, though postherpetic neuralgia can persist.

questions.stem: All statements are true about mycetoma except:

options.label: B
options.text: Surgery is important component of treatment

options.label: D
options.text: Diagnosis can be made by examination of lesion

questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. A) Eumycetoma is caused by bacteria 

 

Mycetoma is a chronic subcutaneous infection caused by either fungi (Eumycetoma) or bacteria (Actinomycetoma). The infection typically affects the foot and is characterized by a clinical triad:

 

  1. Swelling of the affected area, which resembles a tumor.
  2. Discharging sinuses from which pus exudes.
  3. Granules in the pus, often yellow (sulfur granules), indicating colonies of the causative organism.

 

 

  • Eumycetoma is caused by true fungi such as Madurella and Pseudallescheria.
  • Actinomycetoma is caused by bacteria, particularly Nocardia and Actinomadura.

 

The incorrect statement is that "Eumycetoma is caused by bacteria," as it is actually caused by fungi.

 

  • Dapsone therapy post-surgery. 

 

Other Options:

 

Option B. Surgery is an important component of treatment: This is true. Surgical debridement or amputation may be required, especially in advanced cases. Surgery is typically followed by antifungal (for eumycetoma) or antibiotic (for actinomycetoma) therapy.

 

Option C. Usually painless: This is true. Despite the presence of swelling and discharging sinuses, the condition is typically painless unless secondary bacterial infection occurs.

 

Option D. Diagnosis can be made by examination of lesion: This is true. The clinical appearance of swelling, sinuses, and granules is often diagnostic. Examination of the pus and identification of granules can confirm the type of organism involved.

 

Educational Objective:

 

Eumycetoma is caused by fungi, whereas actinomycetoma is caused by bacteria. The clinical triad of mycetoma includes swelling, discharging sinuses, and granules. Surgery is a key component of treatment, and the condition is typically painless.

questions.stemHtml: The insect given in the image below is vector of which of the following disease?
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. D) Visceral leishmaniasis

 

The insect shown in the image is a sand fly (Phlebotomus argentipes), which is the vector for Leishmania donovani, the causative agent of visceral leishmaniasis (kala-azar). Sand flies transmit the promastigote form of the parasite into humans during their bite. Once inside the human host, the promastigote transforms into the amastigote form, which resides within macrophages and spreads to various organs, causing hepatomegaly, splenomegaly, and lymphadenopathy.

 

  • Leishmaniasis forms:
    • Visceral leishmaniasis (kala-azar): Affects internal organs like the liver, spleen, and bone marrow.
    • Cutaneous leishmaniasis: Causes skin ulcers.
    • Mucocutaneous leishmaniasis: Affects mucosal tissues.

 

Endemic areas: This disease is prevalent in regions such as Bihar, Jharkhand (India), and parts of Africa and the Middle East.

 

Other Options:

 

Option A. Japanese Encephalitis (JE): Caused by the Japanese Encephalitis virus, transmitted by Culex mosquitoes, not sand flies.

 

Option B. Trypanosomiasis: Caused by Trypanosoma species and transmitted by the tsetse fly in African trypanosomiasis or by the kissing bug in Chagas disease.

 

Option C. Kyasanur Forest Disease (KFD): Caused by the KFD virus and transmitted by ticks, not sand flies.

 

Educational Objective:

 

The Phlebotomus argentipes (sand fly) is the primary vector of visceral leishmaniasis, transmitting the promastigote form of Leishmania donovani. Remember the unique features of kala-azar: fever, hepatosplenomegaly, and LD (Leishman-Donovan) bodies in macrophages.

questions.stem: XDRTB is defined as:

options.label: D
options.text: Resistant to INH + Rifampicin + Amikacin + Ofloxacin

questions.answerText: Resistant to INH + Rifampicin + Amikacin + Ofloxacin
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. D) Resistant to INH + Rifampicin + Amikacin + Ofloxacin

 

Drug-resistant tuberculosis (TB) is classified into two major types:

 

  1. MDR-TB (Multi-Drug Resistant Tuberculosis):
    • Defined as TB that is resistant to Isoniazid (INH) and Rifampicin (R), the two most powerful first-line anti-TB drugs.
  2. XDR-TB (Extensively Drug Resistant Tuberculosis):
    • Defined as TB that is resistant to Isoniazid (INH), Rifampicin (R), plus any fluoroquinolone (e.g., Ofloxacin, Moxifloxacin), and at least one second-line injectable drug (such as Amikacin, Kanamycin, or Capreomycin).

 

Drug Classifications:

 

  • First-line anti-TB drugs (Group 1):
    • Isoniazid (H), Rifampicin (R), Pyrazinamide (Z), Ethambutol (E)
  • Second-line drugs:
    • Group 2 (Injectables): Amikacin, Kanamycin, Capreomycin, streptomycin.
    • Group 3 (Fluoroquinolones): Ofloxacin, Levofloxacin, Moxifloxacin, Ciprofloxacin

 

 

Other Options:

 

Option A. Resistant to Amikacin + Ofloxacin: This combination is incomplete as it lacks resistance to INH and Rifampicin, making it not fit the definition of XDR-TB.

 

Option B. Resistant to INH + Rifampicin: This defines MDR-TB but does not cover fluoroquinolone or second-line injectable drug resistance required for XDR-TB.

 

Option C. Resistant to INH + Rifampicin + Amikacin: This combination meets the criteria for severe drug resistance but lacks fluoroquinolone resistance, which is essential for defining XDR-TB.

 

Educational Objective:

 

XDR-TB is defined as resistance to Isoniazid (INH), Rifampicin (R), any fluoroquinolone (e.g., Ofloxacin), and one second-line injectable drug (e.g., Amikacin). Proper understanding of drug classifications and resistance patterns is crucial for TB management and treatment.

questions.stem: Wood’s Lamp used in:
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. B) Pityriasis versicolor

 

The Wood’s lamp is an ultraviolet (UV) light that is used in dermatology to detect certain skin infections and conditions by observing characteristic fluorescence. Pityriasis versicolor (also known as Tinea versicolor), caused by Malassezia furfur, is a superficial fungal infection that commonly presents with hypo- or hyperpigmented scaly patches on the skin, along with dandruff (seborrheic dermatitis).

 

  • When examined under Wood’s lamp, Pityriasis versicolor lesions emit a golden-yellow fluorescence due to the presence of fungal pigments.

 

Symptoms of Pityriasis Versicolor:

 

1. Hypopigmented or hyperpigmented patches on the trunk, back, or arms.

 

 

2. Associated dandruff (seborrheic dermatitis).

 

 

Diagnosis of Pityriasis Versicolor:

 

1. Direct Microscopy: Shows the characteristic “spaghetti and meatball” appearance, representing yeast and hyphae forms.

 

 

2. Culture: Shows fried egg colonies on Sabouraud Dextrose Agar (SDA) with added olive oil.

 

 

3. Wood’s Lamp Examination: Reveals golden-yellow fluorescence on affected areas.

 

 

 

Other Options:

 

Option A. Candida: Candida species typically do not fluoresce under UV light and are diagnosed by culture and microscopy.

 

Option C. Sporotrichosis: Caused by Sporothrix schenckii, this subcutaneous mycosis does not fluoresce under Wood’s lamp.

 

Option D. Histoplasma: Histoplasma capsulatum is a systemic dimorphic fungus that does not cause superficial skin lesions or show fluorescence under Wood’s lamp.

 

Educational Objective:

 

Wood’s lamp is most commonly used for diagnosing Pityriasis versicolor, where the characteristic golden-yellow fluorescence is observed. It is also useful in detecting dermatophyte infections (e.g., ringworm) and some bacterial infections, such as erythrasma.

questions.stemHtml: A 15-year-old boy presented with fever and chills for 3 days. On examination he was found to have delayed skin pinch time and dry oral mucosa. A peripheral blood smear revealed the following picture. Identify the pathogen involved:
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. A) Plasmodium falciparum

 

The peripheral blood smear shows ring forms of a parasite inside the red blood cells (RBCs). 

 

The key distinguishing features seen here are:

 

  1. Multiple ring forms within a single RBC.
  2. A headphone-shaped structure (also called "accolé form") within the RBC, characteristic of Plasmodium falciparum.
  • Severe disease manifestations, such as cerebral malaria and multi-organ involvement, are common in falciparum malaria.

 

Other Options:

 

Option B. Babesia: Babesia species can also show ring forms in RBCs but are distinguished by their classic Maltese cross (tetrad) formation, which is absent here. Babesiosis is transmitted by ticks and typically found in the U.S. and Europe.

 

Option C. Plasmodium vivax: P. vivax shows enlarged RBCs with single ring forms and Schüffner's dots (granules). It rarely shows multiple rings within an RBC.

 

Option D. Plasmodium ovale: P. ovale also shows single ring forms within RBCs and fimbriated (oval-shaped) RBCs but does not show multiple ring forms or headphone-shaped structures.

 

Educational Objective:

 

The key features for diagnosing Plasmodium falciparum in a blood smear are:

 

  • Multiple ring forms within a single RBC.
  • Accolé (headphone-shaped) forms.
    These are not seen in other Plasmodium species, making this the distinguishing factor for falciparum malaria.

questions.stem: All are Koch’s postulates except:

options.label: A
options.text: A microorganism should be constantly associated with the lesions of the disease

options.label: B
options.text: It should be possible to isolate the bacterium in pure culture from the lesions

options.label: C
options.text: Inoculation of such pure culture into laboratory animals should reproduce the lesions

options.label: D
options.text: Administration of broad-spectrum antimicrobial agent dependably eradicates the organisms and cures the diseases

questions.answerText: Administration of broad-spectrum antimicrobial agent dependably eradicates the organisms and cures the diseases
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. D) Administration of broad-spectrum antimicrobial agent dependably eradicates the organisms and cures the diseases

 

Koch’s postulates are a set of principles formulated by Robert Koch to establish a causal relationship between a microorganism and a specific disease. These postulates laid the foundation for identifying the microbial causes of infectious diseases.

 

The four postulates are:

 

  1. The microorganism must be found in all organisms suffering from the disease and should not be found in healthy individuals.
  2. The microorganism must be isolated and grown in pure culture.
  3. The cultured microorganism should cause the same disease when introduced into a healthy, susceptible host.
  4. The microorganism must be re-isolated from the experimentally infected host and shown to be the same as the originally identified causative agent.

 

Koch’s postulates:

 

 

The statement "Administration of broad-spectrum antimicrobial agent dependably eradicates the organisms and cures the disease" is unrelated to the proof of causality and does not align with the original postulates.

 

Additional point:

 

Micro-organism not meeting the criteria of Koch’s Postulates

 

 

Educational Objective:

 

Koch's postulates are focused on proving causality between a pathogen and disease by deAmonstrating consistent presence, isolation, reproduction of disease in a new host, and re-isolation. The use of antibiotics or therapeutic intervention is not part of these postulates.

questions.stemHtml: Image depicted below belongs to which of the following?
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. B) Wuchereria bancrofti

 

The parasite in the image is Wuchereria bancrofti, a filarial nematode responsible for causing lymphatic filariasis. The following key features help identify Wuchereria bancrofti:

 

  1. Presence of sheath: The parasite in the image is sheathed, which is a characteristic feature.
  2. Empty tail: The most distinguishing feature of Wuchereria bancrofti is the absence of nuclei in the terminal portion of the tail.

 

Note:

 

Filarial Parasites

 

Seven species

 

  1. Wuchereria bancrofti
  2. Brugia malayi
  3. Loa loa
  4. Onchocerca volvulus
  5. Mansonella ozzardi
  6. M. perstans
  7. M. streptocerca

 

 

Other Options:

 

Option A. Brugia malayi:

 

  • This parasite is also sheathed.
  • However, Brugia malayi has two terminal nuclei at the end of its tail, which distinguishes it from Wuchereria bancrofti.

 

Option C. Loa loa:

 

  • Loa loa is sheathed but contains a continuous line of nuclei throughout the length of its tail, extending to the very tip.
  • This "L for lots of nuclei" mnemonic helps differentiate it from the others.

 

Option D. Onchocerca:

 

  • Onchocerca species are non-sheathed filarial worms.
  • Additionally, they do not have a sheath structure and can be ruled out based on that feature alone.

 

Educational Objective:

 

  • Wuchereria bancrofti is recognized by its sheath and an empty tail without terminal nuclei.
  • The mnemonic "World Bank Limited (WBL)" helps remember the three sheathed filarial species: Wuchereria bancrofti (empty tail), Brugia malayi (two nuclei at the tail), and Loa loa (continuous nuclei to the tip).

questions.stem: A child is presented with fever, conjunctivitis and bluish white spot-on buccal mucosa. Four days later, she developed rashes. What is the characteristic feature of the virus that is responsible for this condition?
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. C) ss- enveloped RNA virus

 

The child described in the question has measles (rubeola virus infection). The key clinical features pointing to this diagnosis include:

 

1. Koplik spots: Small bluish-white spots with a red halo on the buccal mucosa, seen opposite the molars. This is a pathognomonic sign of measles.

 

 

2. Fever and rash progression: The rash typically appears 3-4 days after the initial symptoms and spreads from the face downward.

 

3. Diagnosis: Warthin Finkeldey cells 

 

 

The measles virus belongs to the Paramyxoviridae family.

 

 Important characteristics of the measles virus include:

 

  • Type of genetic material: Single-stranded (ss) RNA.
  • Enveloping: The virus is enveloped.
  • The virus is known for its highly contagious nature and can spread through respiratory droplets.

 

Note:

 

 

Other Options:

 

Option A. ss- naked RNA virus:

 

  • Examples: Picornaviruses (e.g., poliovirus)
  • These viruses are non-enveloped and do not belong to the Paramyxoviridae family.

 

Option B. ds- naked RNA virus:

 

  • There are no double-stranded, naked RNA viruses except for reovirus (e.g., rotavirus), which has a double-stranded RNA genome and is naked.
  • Measles is not double-stranded.

 

Option D. ds- enveloped RNA virus:

 

  • Double-stranded RNA viruses are uncommon, and measles virus is single-stranded, not double-stranded.

 

Educational Objective:

 

  • Measles virus is an ss-RNA virus that is enveloped and belongs to the Paramyxoviridae family.
  • The hallmark of measles is Koplik spots on the buccal mucosa, which are bluish-white spots opposite the molars and appear before the rash develops.

questions.stemHtml: Identify the organism which shows effacement and attachment of intestinal cells as shown below?
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. A) EPEC

 

The image shows the effacement and attachment of intestinal cells, a hallmark feature of Enteropathogenic E. coli (EPEC). EPEC causes diarrhea primarily in infants and young children and has the following key characteristics:

 

  1. Attachment: EPEC bacteria attach to the enterocytes in the small intestine.
  2. Effacement of villi: EPEC leads to the destruction (effacement) and flattening of the intestinal villi, causing a loss of surface area for absorption.
  3. Mechanism of diarrhea: With the villi damaged, absorption in the intestine is impaired, leading to watery diarrhea.

 

The process is characterized by the "attaching and effacing (A/E) lesions" that are diagnostic for EPEC.

 

Note:

 

Enteroinvasive E. coli (EIEC):

 

  • Mechanism: Invasion of intestinal cells.
  • Effect: Causes cell rupture and results in diarrhea with dysentery.

 

Enteroaggressive E. coli (EAEC):

 

  • Mechanism: Secretes unknown toxin (exact mechanism not fully understood).
  • Effect: Causes diarrhea by an unspecified mechanism.

 

 

Other Options:

 

Option B. ETEC (Enterotoxigenic E. coli):

 

  • ETEC causes diarrhea by releasing two types of toxins: heat-labile (LT) and heat-stable (ST) toxins.
  • These toxins increase cyclic AMP (cAMP) and cyclic GMP (cGMP), respectively, leading to fluid loss.
  • ETEC does not cause villous effacement and attachment.

 

Option C. Enterohemorrhagic E. coli (EHEC):

 

  • EHEC also causes "attaching and effacing" lesions, but it differs by releasing Shiga-like toxin (verotoxin).
  • This toxin inhibits protein synthesis, leading to cell death and bloody diarrhea (hemorrhagic colitis).
  • Unlike EPEC, EHEC causes severe complications like hemolytic uremic syndrome (HUS).

 

Option D. Diffusely enteroadherent E. coli (DAEC):

 

  • DAEC adheres to the intestinal mucosa diffusely using multiple pili and fimbriae.
  • Instead of effacement, DAEC strongly adheres, making the mucosa non-functional.

 

Educational objective:

 

EPEC (Enteropathogenic E. coli) causes diarrhea through the effacement of intestinal villi and attachment to intestinal epithelial cells, leading to a loss of absorptive surface area and resulting in watery diarrhea.

questions.stem: Fever with pneumonia, sputum smear showing broad based budding fungi with double contoured cell wall. What is the diagnosis?
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. B) Blastomyces

 

A fungal organism that presents as broad-based budding yeast with a double-contoured cell wall. This is characteristic of Blastomyces dermatitidis.

 

 

A distinctive feature of Blastomyces is its broad-based budding, often described as a "figure of eight" appearance due to the symmetrical attachment of the daughter cell to the parent yeast. The double-walled cell structure further supports this diagnosis. Blastomyces dermatitidis typically causes systemic infections, including pneumonia, especially in endemic regions such as North America.

 

Other Options:

 

Option A. Histoplasma: Histoplasma capsulatum also presents as a budding yeast, but the budding is narrow-based, not broad-based. Additionally, Histoplasma is typically found intracellularly within macrophages and lacks the characteristic double-contoured cell wall seen in Blastomyces.

 

 

Option C. Coccidioides: Coccidioides forms spherules rather than budding yeast. The spherules contain endospores and are not described as having a broad-based budding morphology.

 

Option D. Penicillium marneffei: Penicillium marneffei presents as a yeast with a central septum resembling a "sausage-shaped" appearance. It does not form broad-based budding structures and is generally seen in immunocompromised individuals, particularly in Southeast Asia.

 

Educational Objective:


Blastomyces dermatitidis is identified by its broad-based budding yeast morphology with a double-contoured cell wall, often referred to as the "figure of eight" appearance. This feature differentiates it from other yeasts, such as Histoplasma (narrow-based budding, intracellular) and Coccidioides (spherules instead of budding yeast).

questions.stemHtml: A patient with benign hypertrophy of prostate was admitted in the hospital for 3 weeks. He subsequently developed suspected catheter associated-urinary tract infection. The tip of the catheter was sent for culture and was grown on blood agar. After 24 hours, the blood agar shows the following appearance. What is the likely causative agent for the UTI?
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. A) Proteus mirabilis

 

The blood agar plate shows concentric rings of bacterial growth, which is characteristic of swarming motility. Swarming motility describes the rapid movement of bacteria across the agar surface, forming distinctive concentric waves or a "swarming" pattern. Proteus mirabilis is a gram-negative, motile bacterium commonly associated with catheter-associated urinary tract infections (CA-UTI). Its swarming motility is due to its peritrichous flagella, which enable rapid surface movement.

 

This bacterium is also associated with an increased likelihood of struvite stone formation due to its urease production, which alkalinizes the urine.

 

Note:

 

Types of Motility:

 

• Darting- V. cholera, Campylobactor

 

 

• Tumbling - Listeria at 25°C

 

 

• Cork screw - T. pallidum

 

 

• Swarming - P. mirabilis, P. vulgaris, CI. tetani, Bacillus cereus

 

 

Other Options:

 

Option B. Pseudomonas: Although Pseudomonas aeruginosa is a motile bacterium known for its characteristic green pigment and fruity odor, it does not exhibit swarming motility in this distinctive concentric pattern. Instead, it forms flat, irregular colonies.

 

Option C. Escherichia coli: E. coli is the most common cause of UTIs, but it does not show swarming motility. Instead, it forms round, smooth, and convex colonies on blood agar.

 

Option D. Klebsiella pneumoniae: Klebsiella species are non-motile, encapsulated bacteria. Their colonies appear mucoid due to the capsule, and they do not demonstrate swarming motility.

 

Educational Objective:

 

Proteus mirabilis is a motile bacterium that exhibits swarming motility, forming concentric waves on agar plates. It is a frequent cause of catheter-associated urinary tract infections (CA-UTIs), particularly in patients with indwelling catheters.

questions.stem: Correct sequence of bacterial growth curve:

options.label: A
options.text: Log phase – Lag Phase – Stationary phase – Decline phase

options.label: B
options.text: Lag Phase – Log phase – Stationary phase – Decline phase

options.label: C
options.text: Stationary phase – Log phase – Lag Phase – Decline phase

options.label: D
options.text: Lag phase – Stationary phase – Log phase – Decline phase

questions.answerText: Lag Phase – Log phase – Stationary phase – Decline phase
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. B) Lag Phase – Log phase – Stationary phase – Decline phase

 

The bacterial growth curve describes the four distinct phases of growth observed in a closed system (such as a culture media) over time. 

 

The correct sequence of these phases is as follows:

 

 

 

  1. Lag phase: In this phase, bacteria are metabolically active but not dividing. They are adjusting to the new environment, synthesizing enzymes, and preparing for cell division. The cell size may increase, but the population remains constant.
  2. Log phase (exponential phase): Bacteria divide at a constant rate, leading to exponential growth. During this phase, the number of bacteria increases rapidly, and the cell size may return to normal. This phase represents maximum metabolic activity.
  3. Stationary phase: Nutrients become limited, and waste products accumulate. The rate of cell division equals the rate of cell death, resulting in a stable population size. This phase may also see the formation of spores or exotoxins in some bacteria.
  4. Decline phase (death phase): Nutrients are depleted, and toxic waste products accumulate, causing bacteria to die at an accelerated rate. This phase is characterized by a decrease in the viable bacterial population and the presence of involutionary (abnormal) forms of bacteria.

 

Educational Objective:

 

The correct sequence of the bacterial growth curve is lag phase, log (exponential) phase, stationary phase, and decline phase. Each phase has specific characteristics: preparation and adaptation in lag phase, rapid division in log phase, equilibrium in stationary phase, and bacterial death in the decline phase.

questions.stem: Eggs of which of the following parasite cause intense pruritus in perianal skin:
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. C) Enterobius vermicularis

 

The correct answer is Enterobius vermicularis, commonly known as the pinworm. The characteristic symptom of infection by Enterobius vermicularis is intense perianal itching (pruritus), especially at night. This is caused by the gravid (pregnant) female worms migrating out of the rectum at night to lay eggs around the anal opening. The irritation from these eggs triggers intense pruritus.

 

 

Key points about the egg:

 

  • Shape: Planoconvex (flattened on one side and convex on the other)
  • Color: Non-bile stained (transparent)
  • Content: Contains a tadpole-like larva

 

 

The infection is common in children and is easily transmitted due to scratching, as the eggs can spread to surfaces, clothing, and fingernails.

 

Other Options:

 

Option A. Ascaris: Ascaris lumbricoides causes ascariasis, but it does not lead to perianal itching. Instead, it typically causes abdominal pain, malnutrition, and pulmonary symptoms during the larval migration phase.

 

Option B. Hookworm: Hookworms (Ancylostoma duodenale and Necator americanus) cause skin irritation at the site of larval penetration (commonly known as "ground itch") but do not cause pruritus around the perianal region. The primary symptoms are iron-deficiency anemia and gastrointestinal discomfort.

 

Option D. Trichuris: Trichuris trichiura (whipworm) infections typically result in diarrhea, rectal prolapse, and anemia in heavy infections but not perianal pruritus.

 

Educational Objective:

 

Enterobius vermicularis causes nocturnal perianal pruritus due to gravid females laying eggs around the anal opening at night. The characteristic eggs are planoconvex, non-bile stained, and transparent.

questions.stemHtml: A 33-year-old sexually active male is having urethral discharge since last 8 months along with burning sensation while micturition. Gram staining smear of urethral swab Sample is showing following picture. The causative organism is:
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. B) Neisseria gonorrhoeae


In this case, the Gram-stained smear reveals intracellular Gram-negative cocci (appearing as red spherical dots) present inside neutrophils. This characteristic finding is indicative of Neisseria gonorrhoeae infection, which is a Gram-negative diplococcus that often resides within polymorphonuclear neutrophils (PMNs). The typical symptoms include urethral discharge, dysuria (pain during urination), and pruritus. Neisseria gonorrhoeae is a common cause of sexually transmitted urethritis in men and cervicitis in women.

 

The life cycle of Neisseria gonorrhoeae involves direct transmission through sexual contact, and it colonizes the mucosal surfaces of the genitourinary tract, leading to an intense inflammatory response.

 

NOTE:

 

 

Other Options:

 

Option A. Chlamydia trachomatis: Although Chlamydia trachomatis also causes urethritis, it is not visible on Gram stain because it is an intracellular organism that lacks a peptidoglycan cell wall, making it poorly stained. Instead, Chlamydia is often detected using nucleic acid amplification tests (NAATs).

 

Option C. Mycoplasma hominis: Mycoplasma hominis lacks a cell wall entirely and does not stain with Gram stain. It is associated with non-gonococcal urethritis rather than gonococcal urethritis and is not intracellular cocci visible in this way.

 

Option D. Ureaplasma urealyticum: Similar to Mycoplasma, Ureaplasma urealyticum also lacks a cell wall and is not detectable on Gram staining. It is associated with milder cases of non-gonococcal urethritis.

 

Educational Objective:

 

Neisseria gonorrhoeae appears as intracellular, Gram-negative, kidney-shaped cocci (diplococci) inside neutrophils on Gram stain and is a common cause of sexually transmitted urethritis.

questions.stem: Which of this need V factor?
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. C) H. paraphrophilus

 

Haemophilus species require specific growth factors that are present in blood:

 

  • Factor V (NAD) – found in yeast extracts, some blood components, and actively growing Staphylococcus aureus colonies.
  • Factor X (hemin) – derived from blood and required for the synthesis of cytochromes.

 

The mnemonic helps to remember:

 

  • Only Factor X (10) is required by "Ducreyi" (D for Ducreyi, D for "Das" meaning 10 in Hindi).
  • Only Factor V (5) is required by all "Para" species (P for Para, P for "Paanch" meaning 5 in Hindi). These include H. parainfluenzae, H. parahaemolyticus, and H. paraphrophilus.
  • Both Factors V and X are required by "HAI": H. influenzae, H. aegyptius, and H. haemolyticus.

 

For H. paraphrophilus, as indicated by its prefix "Para," only Factor V (NAD) is required.

 

Other Options:

 

Option A. H. influenzae: Requires both Factor V and X (NAD and hemin). It causes respiratory infections such as pneumonia, meningitis, and otitis media.

 

Option B. H. ducreyi: Requires only Factor X (hemin). It causes chancroid, a sexually transmitted infection characterized by painful genital ulcers.

 

Option D. H. aegyptius: Requires both Factor V and X. It causes conjunctivitis, also known as "pink eye."

 

Educational Objective:

 

Haemophilus paraphrophilus requires only Factor V (NAD) for growth, whereas other Haemophilus species may require Factor X (hemin), or both Factors V and X.

questions.stem: HBV and HDV false is:

options.label: B
options.text: HDV causes more serious infection d/t superinfection

options.label: C
options.text: HDV cannot infect in absence of HBV

questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. D) HDV is a DNA virus

 

Hepatitis D virus (HDV), also called delta virus, is a defective RNA virus that requires the presence of hepatitis B virus (HBV) for its replication and transmission. HDV uses the HBsAg (hepatitis B surface antigen) as an envelope for entry and assembly, meaning HDV cannot cause infection on its own without HBV.

 

There are two types of HDV infections:

 

1. Co-infection: HBV and HDV infect simultaneously in a previously uninfected person. This leads to acute hepatitis with a high chance of recovery and a lower chance of chronic hepatitis.

 

 

2. Superinfection: HDV infects a person who is already a carrier of HBV. This type of infection is more severe and has a higher likelihood of leading to chronic and fulminant hepatitis, as the immune system is already compromised. Chronic infection rates in superinfection can be as high as 80%, making it much more dangerous.

 

The given statement "HDV is a DNA virus" is false because HDV is an RNA virus, unlike HBV, which is a DNA virus.

 

Other Options:

 

Option A. Both can infect simultaneously: True. HBV and HDV can co-infect a person at the same time, leading to co-infection. This usually results in an acute hepatitis episode but with a lower chance of chronicity.

 

Option B. HDV causes more serious infection due to superinfection: True. In superinfection, HDV infects someone already infected with HBV, leading to more severe liver damage, often resulting in chronic hepatitis or fulminant liver failure.

 

Option C. HDV cannot infect in the absence of HBV: True. HDV is a defective virus and cannot replicate or infect without the presence of hepatitis B virus. It requires HBsAg for its envelope formation.

 

Educational Objective:


Hepatitis D virus (HDV) is an RNA virus that requires HBV for its replication and is more dangerous in the case of superinfection, with a high rate of chronic hepatitis.

questions.stemHtml: A 23-year-old female presents with fever and altered sensorium for two days with the following rash on legs. Her BP is 70/50 mm Hg and neck stiffness is present. Lumbar puncture reveals cloudy turbid CSF with 4200 cells/uL, Protein level 168 and Glucose of 21 mg/dL. Which of the following correctly describes the organism causing this condition?

options.label: A
options.text: Gram Negative Diplococci (kidney shaped), Oxidase positive

options.label: B
options.text: Gram Negative Diplococci, ferments glucose and maltose

options.label: C
options.text: Gram Positive cocci catalase negative, bacitracin sensitive

options.label: D
options.text: Gram Positive Diplococci (lanceolate), catalase negative, optochin sensitive

questions.answerText: Gram Negative Diplococci, ferments glucose and maltose
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. B) Gram Negative Diplococci, ferments glucose and maltose

 

This is a classic presentation of bacterial meningitis caused by Neisseria meningitidis. The patient presents with a purpuric rash, shock (BP 70/50 mmHg), altered sensorium, fever, and neck stiffness—all hallmark signs of meningococcemia with meningitis.

 

  • Cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) findings indicate bacterial meningitis:
    • Cloudy appearance due to pus (indicating infection).
    • Elevated protein (168 mg/dL), suggestive of increased permeability due to inflammation.
    • Low glucose (21 mg/dL) because bacteria consume glucose in the CSF.

 

The organism in question is Neisseria meningitidis, a gram-negative diplococcus that appears kidney- or half-moon-shaped and is both oxidase positive and capable of fermenting glucose and maltose.

 

The associated rash with septicemia and disseminated intravascular coagulation (DIC) is characteristic of Waterhouse-Friderichsen syndrome, a severe complication of meningococcemia, which leads to adrenal hemorrhage, shock, and multiorgan failure.

 

NOTE:

 

 

 

Other Options:

 

Option A. Gram-negative diplococci (kidney-shaped), oxidase positive: True for Neisseria species, but this description alone does not distinguish between N. gonorrhoeae and N. meningitidis.

 

Option C. Gram-positive cocci catalase negative, bacitracin sensitive: Refers to Streptococcus pyogenes, a causative agent of pharyngitis, cellulitis, and rheumatic fever, but it does not cause purpuric rashes associated with meningitis.

 

Option D. Gram-positive diplococci (lanceolate), catalase negative, optochin sensitive: Describes Streptococcus pneumoniae, another common cause of meningitis. However, it presents differently, typically without purpuric rashes and DIC.

 

Educational Objective:

 

Neisseria meningitidis is a gram-negative diplococcus that ferments both glucose and maltose, is oxidase positive, and can cause fulminant bacterial meningitis with purpuric rash, septic shock, and Waterhouse-Friderichsen syndrome.

questions.stem: Helminth implicated in causing pernicious anemia is:
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. A) Diphyllobothrium latum

 

Diphyllobothrium latum, also known as the fish tapeworm, is a cestode that can cause pernicious anemia. This parasite competes with the host for vitamin B12 in the intestine, leading to vitamin B12 deficiency and resulting in megaloblastic (pernicious) anemia.

 

Life Cycle of Diphyllobothrium latum:

 

  1. Definitive host: Humans (where the adult worm resides and releases eggs).
  2. First intermediate host: Cyclops (a type of crustacean) that ingests the larval form (L1 stage).
  3. Second intermediate host: Freshwater fish that consume the cyclops, allowing the larva to develop into the infective L3 larva (pleurocercoid stage).
  4. Transmission to humans: Occurs when humans eat undercooked or raw fish containing the L3 larva.

 

 

In the human intestine, the larva matures into an adult worm, which absorbs large amounts of vitamin B12, leading to the deficiency that causes pernicious anemia.

 

Other Options:

 

Option B. Ascaris: Ascaris lumbricoides is a roundworm that primarily causes intestinal obstruction and respiratory symptoms during its migration. It does not cause vitamin B12 deficiency or anemia.

 

Option C. Taenia solium: Taenia solium is a pork tapeworm that can cause taeniasis and cysticercosis, but it does not cause vitamin B12 deficiency or pernicious anemia.

 

Option D. Hymenolepis nana: This is the dwarf tapeworm, commonly associated with mild gastrointestinal symptoms. It does not cause anemia or vitamin B12 deficiency.

 

Educational Objective:

 

Diphyllobothrium latum, the fish tapeworm, is the only helminth known to cause vitamin B12 deficiency and pernicious anemia due to its absorption of vitamin B12 in the intestine.

questions.stem: Nontoxigenic C. diphtheriae changes to toxigenic C. diphtheriae by the help of bacteriophage. By which method this conversion occur?
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. D) lysogenic Conversion

 

The process by which a non-toxigenic strain of Corynebacterium diphtheriae becomes toxigenic involves the acquisition of the tox gene through the integration of a bacteriophage (virus) called β-phage. This phage carries the tox gene responsible for diphtheria toxin production. When the bacteriophage injects its genetic material into the bacterium, it integrates into the bacterial chromosome, making the bacterium capable of producing the diphtheria toxin.

 

 

This process is known as lysogenic conversion, where the bacteriophage DNA integrates into the bacterial genome and remains dormant, but its genes (such as the tox gene) can be expressed by the host bacterium, converting a non-toxigenic bacterium into a toxigenic one.

 

Other Methods of Gene Transfer:

 

Option A. Transfection: Refers to the introduction of naked DNA into a bacterial cell, usually performed artificially in a laboratory.

 

Option B. Transduction: Involves the transfer of bacterial DNA by a bacteriophage from one bacterium to another, functioning as a "pick and drop" mechanism. The phage does not insert its own genetic material but transfers DNA from one bacterium to another.

 

Option C. Conjugation: Refers to the direct transfer of DNA from one bacterium to another through physical contact via a pilus. This method is often used by plasmid DNA for horizontal gene transfer.

 

Educational Objective:

 

Lysogenic conversion occurs when a bacteriophage integrates its genetic material into the bacterial chromosome, such as in Corynebacterium diphtheriae, converting it into a toxigenic strain capable of producing diphtheria toxin.

questions.stemHtml: Identify the vector involved in the spread of disease, whose peripheral smear is as given:
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. A) Ixodid tick

 

The peripheral blood smear shows Maltese cross formations inside red blood cells (RBCs). The Maltese cross is a diagnostic feature of Babesia infection, caused by protozoan parasites of the genus Babesia. This condition is known as babesiosis.

 

Key Features of Babesiosis:

 

  • Maltese cross: Formed by the tetrad arrangement of merozoites within RBCs.
  • Symptoms include fever, hemolytic anemia, fatigue, and hepatosplenomegaly.
  • The vector responsible for transmission is the Ixodid tick (hard tick), specifically Ixodes scapularis (the same tick responsible for Lyme disease transmission).

 

Life Cycle of Babesia:

 

The life cycle of Babesia is similar to Plasmodium (malaria), but Babesia lacks the exoerythrocytic (liver stage) cycle, and humans are dead-end hosts in the transmission cycle.

 

Other Options:

 

Option B. Anopheles: Anopheles mosquito is the vector for Plasmodium species, which cause malaria. Malaria does not show Maltese cross but shows ring forms, schizonts, and gametocytes in blood smears.

 

Option C. Louse: Lice are responsible for spreading diseases such as epidemic typhus (Rickettsia prowazekii) and relapsing fever (Borrelia recurrentis) but not Babesia infection.

 

Option D. Sandfly: Sandflies transmit Leishmania species, causing leishmaniasis (cutaneous, mucocutaneous, and visceral forms), which shows amastigotes in tissue smears, not blood smears.

 

Educational Objective:

 

The Ixodid tick (Ixodes species) transmits Babesia parasites, which form the characteristic Maltese cross inside RBCs, leading to babesiosis.

questions.stem: A person has received complete immunization against tetanus 10 years ago. Now he presents with a clean wound without any lacerations from an injury sustained 2.5 hours ago. He should now be given:

options.label: D
options.text: Human Tet globulin and single dose of toxoid

questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. B) Single dose of tetanus toxoid

 

In the management of wounds, it is crucial to assess both the type of wound (clean or dirty) and the immunization history.

 

Tetanus Wound Classification:

 

  1. Non-Tetanus Prone Wound:
    • Superficial, clean wounds less than 1 cm in depth.
    • No contamination with soil, dirt, or feces.
    • Age of the wound is less than 6 hours.
  2. Tetanus Prone Wound:
    • Deep wound (more than 1 cm), lacerated, or punctured.
    • Contaminated with dirt, soil, feces, or pus.
    • Older wounds (more than 6 hours).

 

Immunization Schedule for Tetanus:

 

 

Case Analysis:

 

In this case:

 

  • The patient received complete immunization 10 years ago.
  • The wound is clean and occurred 2.5 hours ago (fresh wound).
  • Since it is a non-tetanus prone wound and the last immunization was more than 10 years ago, the recommendation is a single dose of tetanus toxoid to boost immunity.

 

No tetanus immunoglobulin is required because the wound is not prone to tetanus infection.

 

Other Options:

 

Option A. Full course of tetanus toxoid: Not needed since the patient has already received prior complete immunization.

 

Option C. Human tetanus globulin: Not necessary for clean, non-tetanus prone wounds.

 

Option D. Human tetanus globulin and single dose of toxoid: This is required only for tetanus-prone wounds if the last dose was taken more than 10 years ago.

 

Educational Objective:

 

A single dose of tetanus toxoid is sufficient for clean, non-tetanus prone wounds if the last tetanus dose was taken more than 10 years ago.

questions.stem: Staph. aureus causes vomiting in 6–8 hours. The mechanism of action is:
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. B) Vagal stimulation

 

Staphylococcus aureus food poisoning occurs due to the ingestion of pre-formed enterotoxin. The incubation period is short (2–6 hours) since the toxin is already synthesized and present in the food. Common food items involved include dairy products (milk, cream, cheese), meat, and fish.

 

The Staphylococcal enterotoxin is a superantigen that directly stimulates the vomiting center in the brain by binding to vagal nerve endings in the gastrointestinal tract. This stimulation leads to:

 

  1. Vomiting due to activation of the brain’s vomiting center.
  2. Diarrhea due to increased vagal stimulation causing parasympathetic activation, leading to increased gut motility.

 

Since the toxin acts directly, symptoms appear rapidly.

 

Other Options:

 

Option A. Stimulation of cAMP: This mechanism is seen in toxins like cholera toxin and heat-labile toxin of E. coli, which cause secretory diarrhea by increasing intracellular cAMP levels in enterocytes.

 

Option C. Stimulation of cGMP: This mechanism is seen in the heat-stable toxin of E. coli, which increases cGMP, leading to diarrhea.

 

Option D. Acts through ganglioside GM receptor: This is the mechanism of cholera toxin and Shiga toxin in host cells.

 

Educational Objective:

 

Staphylococcus aureus food poisoning involves pre-formed enterotoxin that rapidly stimulates the vomiting center and vagus nerve, causing vomiting and diarrhea within a few hours of ingesting contaminated food.

questions.stem: A neonate has hepatosplenomegaly. His urine was stained with Giemsa stain which revealed owl’s eye appearance inclusions. Which will be the most probable cause?
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. A) CMV

 

Cytomegalovirus (CMV) is a DNA virus from the Herpesviridae family. The presence of owl’s eye inclusion bodies in stained samples is a characteristic finding in CMV infections. These inclusions represent large, eosinophilic nuclear inclusions with a halo around them, resembling an "owl’s eye."

 

Congenital CMV Infection:

 

  • Clinical Features:
    • Hepatosplenomegaly
    • Jaundice
    • Microcephaly
    • Sensorineural hearing loss
    • Periventricular calcifications

 

 

  • Diagnosis:
    • Giemsa or Papanicolaou stain of body fluids (urine, saliva) shows characteristic owl’s eye inclusions.

 

 

  • PCR and viral cultures confirm CMV DNA presence.

 

Other Options:

 

Option B. HIV: Congenital HIV infection typically presents with failure to thrive, recurrent infections, and immunodeficiency. It does not show "owl’s eye" inclusions.

 

Option C. Rubella: Congenital rubella presents with the classic triad of cataracts, cardiac defects (PDA), and sensorineural deafness. No "owl’s eye" inclusions are seen.

 

Option D. Measles: Measles virus infection shows Warthin-Finkeldey giant cells in lymphoid tissue, not owl’s eye inclusions.

 

Educational Objective:


The presence of owl’s eye inclusions in Giemsa-stained samples, combined with hepatosplenomegaly in a neonate, is characteristic of congenital CMV infection.

questions.stem: Reduviid bug is a vector for the transmission of:
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. D) Chagas disease

 

The Reduviid bug (also called the "kissing bug") is the vector for Chagas disease, which is caused by the protozoan Trypanosoma cruzi. The infection occurs when the feces of the Reduviid bug, which contain the infective trypomastigote form of the parasite, are deposited on the skin. The person often becomes infected by rubbing the feces into the bite wound or mucous membranes, such as the eyes.

 

Key Clinical Features of Chagas Disease:

 

  • Early stage:
    • Chagoma: A localized swelling at the site of infection.
    • Romana’s sign: Unilateral conjunctivitis and swelling of the eyelid due to rubbing the infected feces into the eye.

 

 

  • Late stage:
    • Cardiac involvement: Myocarditis leading to dilated cardiomyopathy.
    • Megaesophagus and megacolon: Due to damage to the autonomic nervous system controlling the gastrointestinal tract.

 

Geographic Distribution:

 

  • Chagas disease is primarily found in South and Central America, where the Reduviid bug is endemic.

 

Other Options:

 

Option A. Relapsing fever: Caused by Borrelia species and transmitted by lice (epidemic relapsing fever) or ticks (endemic relapsing fever), not by Reduviid bugs.

 

Option B. Lyme disease: Caused by Borrelia burgdorferi and transmitted by the Ixodes tick (deer tick), not by Reduviid bugs.

 

Option C. Scrub typhus: Caused by Orientia tsutsugamushi and transmitted by chigger mites (larvae of trombiculid mites), not by Reduviid bugs.

 

Difference Between Trypanosoma cruzi and Trypanosoma brucei

 

Here’s a comparison based on the transcript details:

 

 

  1. Trypanosoma brucei gambiense: causes chronic form of sleeping sickness.
  2. Trypanosoma brucei rhodesiense: causes acute form. | Chronic and acute forms of Chagas disease (chronic form causes long-term organ damage). |
    | Endemicity | Endemic to Africa | Endemic to South and Central America |
    | Reservoir Host | Wild animals such as antelopes | Wild animals such as armadillos and opossums |

 

Mnemonic:

 

  • American = Cruzi ("C" for Crazy Americans with Chagas)
  • African = Brucei ("B" for Brain involvement in Sleeping Sickness)

 

Educational Objective:

 

Chagas disease is caused by Trypanosoma cruzi and is transmitted by the Reduviid bug (kissing bug) through its infected feces, leading to early-stage chagoma or Romana's sign and late-stage cardiac and gastrointestinal complications.

questions.stem: A farmer presenting with fever off and on for the past 4 years was diagnosed to be suffering from chronic brucellosis. All of the following serological tests would be helpful in the diagnosis at this state except:
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. A) Standard Agglutination test

 

Brucellosis is a zoonotic disease that presents with undulating fever (fever that comes and goes), arthritis, and hepatosplenomegaly. Chronic brucellosis is a long-standing infection, often found in farmers and others exposed to livestock.

 

The Standard Agglutination Test (SAT) is the primary test used for initial diagnosis of brucellosis, but it cannot distinguish between acute and chronic infections. SAT detects the presence of antibodies but does not differentiate between IgM (acute) and IgG (chronic) antibodies. Since this patient has been symptomatic for four years, SAT is not useful at this chronic stage as it will likely still detect antibodies without distinguishing the phase of infection.

 

Other Options:

 

Serological Tests for Chronic Brucellosis:

 

Option B. 2-Mercaptoethanol Test: Helps differentiate between IgM (acute phase) and IgG (chronic phase) antibodies. The chemical 2-mercaptoethanol destroys IgM antibodies, allowing IgG levels to be assessed. If the test remains positive after treatment with 2-ME, it indicates chronic infection (due to IgG persistence). Mnemonic: M kills M (Mercaptoethanol kills IgM).

 

Option C. Complement Fixation Test: Measures IgG antibodies and is useful for detecting chronic brucellosis.

 

Option D. Coomb’s Test: Detects incomplete (blocking) antibodies, which are typically seen in chronic brucellosis cases.

 

Educational Objective:

 

The Standard Agglutination Test (SAT) is useful for initial diagnosis but cannot differentiate between acute and chronic brucellosis. In chronic brucellosis, tests like 2-Mercaptoethanol (2-ME) test, Complement Fixation Test (CFT), and Coombs Test are used.

questions.stem: A farmer who is also having dairy farm with history of handling cows, presented to the dermatology OPD with ulcer over forearm with central black eschar. True statement regarding the likely causative organism:
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. B) McFadyean's reaction positive

 

The clinical presentation of a painless ulcer with a central black eschar in a farmer handling animals points toward cutaneous anthrax, caused by Bacillus anthracis. Anthrax is a zoonotic disease commonly acquired by contact with infected animals or their products.

 

Diagnostic Features of Bacillus anthracis:

 

1. Nutrient Agar:

 

  • Colony appearance resembles curly "Medusa’s head" due to curly projections of growth.

 

 

2. Gelatin Stab Test:

 

  • Shows inverted fir-tree appearance due to liquefaction at the surface where oxygen concentration is high.

 

 

3. Solid Media Containing Penicillin:

 

  • Shows string of pearls appearance (due to the inhibition of bacterial cell wall synthesis by penicillin).

 

 

4. Polychrome Methylene Blue Staining (McFadyean's Reaction):

 

  • Stains the polypeptide capsule of Bacillus anthracis, causing it to separate from the bacterium and form amorphous clumps.
  • The bacteria form bamboo stick appearance (resembling train bogies), with the capsule surrounding them.

 

 

Mac-Fadyean's Rx

 

5. Selective medium → PLET medium

 

  1. Polymyxin
  2. Lysozyme
  3. Ethylene diamine tetracetic acid (EDTA)
  4. Thallous acetate

 

 

Other Options:

 

Option A. Coagulase positive: Refers to Staphylococcus aureus, which can cause abscesses and furuncles but does not cause black eschar with painless ulcers.

 

Option C. Nagler’s positive: Refers to Clostridium perfringens, which is identified using the Nagler's reaction (detects alpha toxin activity). Clostridium perfringens is associated with gas gangrene, not cutaneous anthrax.

 

Option D. Satellitism positive: Refers to Haemophilus influenzae, which shows satellite growth around colonies of Staphylococcus aureus due to NAD (Factor V) production by Staph. This is unrelated to Bacillus anthracis.

 

Educational Objective:

 

The McFadyean's reaction is a key diagnostic test for anthrax, showing separation of the bacterial capsule from the body of Bacillus anthracis when stained with polychrome methylene blue, giving a characteristic "capsule clump" appearance.

questions.stemHtml: A Female had a thorn prick 5 years ago. She presented with a slowly growing 2 × 2 cm verrucous lesion which on KOH mount showed the following image?
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. D) Chromoblastomycosis

 

The history of a thorn prick, followed by a slow-growing verrucous (warty/cauliflower-like) lesion over 5 years, is highly indicative of subcutaneous fungal infection. The KOH mount shows characteristic brown-colored, spherical, yeast-like cells with septa, often arranged like copper pennies (also known as sclerotic bodies or Medlar bodies).

 

 

Key Features of Chromoblastomycosis:

 

  • Causative agents: Fonsecaea pedrosoi, Cladophialophora carrionii, and others.
  • Transmission: Entry via skin trauma (e.g., thorn prick).
  • Characteristic lesion: Slowly progressive, warty, cauliflower-like lesion.
  • Microscopic finding: Copper penny appearance or sclerotic bodies seen on KOH mount or histopathology.

 

Other Names for Sclerotic Bodies:

 

  • Copper penny bodies
  • Medlar bodies

 

Other Options:

 

Option A. Phaeohyphomycosis: This condition also involves dematiaceous (darkly pigmented) fungi but typically presents with cystic or nodular lesions rather than a warty, cauliflower-like growth.

 

Option B. Blastomycosis: Blastomycosis is caused by Blastomyces dermatitidis and typically causes pulmonary involvement and cutaneous ulcers but not characteristic copper penny bodies.

 

Option C. Sporotrichosis: Caused by Sporothrix schenckii, sporotrichosis is known as rose gardener’s disease. It presents with nodular lesions that spread along lymphatic channels, forming a "chain of nodules" rather than warty verrucous growths.

 

 

Educational Objective:

 

The presence of a slow-growing verrucous lesion, history of thorn prick, and copper penny appearance (sclerotic bodies) on KOH mount are diagnostic of chromoblastomycosis, a subcutaneous fungal infection caused by pigmented fungi.

questions.stem: Which HPV causes Condyloma acuminate. Most common cause?
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. B) HPV 6 &11

 

Condyloma Acuminata refers to genital warts, which are caused by low-risk strains of Human Papilloma Virus (HPV). The most common HPV types responsible for benign genital warts are HPV 6 and 11. These strains cause cauliflower-like lesions in the genital region but are non-oncogenic and do not cause malignant transformation.

 

Types of HPV and Associated Conditions:

 

  • Low-risk HPV types (benign warts):
    • HPV 6 and 11: Cause condyloma acuminata (genital warts) and recurrent respiratory papillomatosis.

 

 

  • These types are referred to as non-oncogenic (low-risk) HPV.
  • High-risk HPV types (malignant cancers):
    • HPV 16 and 18: Most common types associated with cervical, anal, penile, vulvar, and oropharyngeal cancers.
    • Other high-risk types include 31, 33, 45, 52, and 58.
    • HPV 16 and 18 are responsible for the majority of cervical cancers.

 

Other Options:

 

Option A. HPV 1-4: These types cause cutaneous warts on hands and feet (common and plantar warts).

 

Option C. HPV 16 & 18: High-risk types associated with cervical, penile, and anogenital cancers.

 

Option D. HPV 31 & 33: High-risk types that are also associated with malignant transformations but less commonly than 16 and 18.

 

Educational Objective:

 

HPV 6 and 11 are responsible for condyloma acuminata (genital warts), which present as warty, cauliflower-like lesions in the genital area. These strains are non-oncogenic and do not cause cancer.

questions.stem: Winter bottom sign is seen in:
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. A) African trypanosomiasis

 

Winter bottom’s sign refers to posterior cervical lymphadenopathy (swelling of the lymph nodes at the back of the neck). It is a classic clinical feature of African trypanosomiasis (also known as sleeping sickness) caused by Trypanosoma brucei. The infection is transmitted by the Tsetse fly (Glossina spp.).

 

 

Key Features of African Trypanosomiasis:

 

  • Causative organism: Trypanosoma brucei gambiense (chronic form) and Trypanosoma brucei rhodesiense (acute form).
  • Vector: Tsetse fly (saliva contains infective trypomastigotes).
  • Clinical presentation:
    • Early sign: Chancre at the site of the Tsetse fly bite.
    • Winterbottom’s sign: Posterior cervical lymphadenopathy.
    • Late-stage disease: CNS involvement leading to sleeping sickness (excessive daytime sleepiness and altered mental status).

 

Other Options:

 

Option B. American trypanosomiasis: Caused by Trypanosoma cruzi and transmitted by the Reduviid bug (kissing bug). The early clinical feature is Romana’s sign (unilateral eyelid swelling), not Winterbottom’s sign.

 

Option C. Leishmaniasis: Caused by Leishmania donovani (visceral leishmaniasis), L. tropica (cutaneous leishmaniasis), and L. braziliensis (mucocutaneous leishmaniasis). The diagnostic feature is LD bodies (Leishman-Donovan bodies) seen in macrophages.

 

Option D. Toxoplasmosis: Caused by Toxoplasma gondii, toxoplasmosis presents with lymphadenopathy but not specific to the posterior cervical nodes.

 

Educational Objective:

 

Winter bottom’s sign (posterior cervical lymphadenopathy) is a hallmark feature of African trypanosomiasis caused by Trypanosoma brucei and transmitted by the Tsetse fly.

questions.stem: To prevent swarming the % agar in Nutrient agar has to be increased at least to:
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. C) 6%

 

Swarming is a phenomenon where bacteria exhibit rapid, coordinated movement across the surface of solid media, forming characteristic concentric wave-like patterns. Bacteria like Proteus species, Clostridium tetani, and Bacillus cereus are known for swarming behavior.

 

Swarming Inhibition:

 

To inhibit swarming, the medium must be made stony hard by increasing the percentage of agar:

 

 

  • 0.5% agar: Semi-solid (used for motility tests).
  • 2% agar: Solid medium (standard for routine cultures).
  • 6% agar: Stony hard (prevents swarming by providing a firm surface).

 

By increasing the agar concentration to 6%, the solidified medium becomes so firm that bacteria like Proteus spp. cannot swarm across it.

 

Educational Objective:

 

To prevent swarming motility of bacteria like Proteus spp., increase the agar concentration to 6%, making the surface stony hard and resistant to bacterial movement.

questions.stem: A chronic alcoholic patient is presented with necrotic pneumonia. Sputum culture reveals mucoid lactose fermenting colonies on MacConkey medium. What is the organism?
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. A) Klebsiella

 

The history of a chronic alcoholic presenting with necrotic pneumonia (common for aspiration pneumonia) combined with mucoid lactose-fermenting colonies on MacConkey agar strongly suggests Klebsiella pneumoniae.

 

Key Characteristics of Klebsiella pneumoniae:

 

  • Lactose-fermenting: Forms pink colonies on MacConkey agar due to lactose fermentation.

 

 

  • Mucoid appearance: Colonies appear shiny, sticky, and mucoid due to the thick polysaccharide capsule.
  • Clinical association: Commonly seen in chronic alcoholics, diabetics, and immunocompromised individuals.
  • Infection: Causes necrotizing pneumonia with characteristic "currant jelly sputum" (due to hemoptysis and mucus).

 

Classification of Enterobacteriaceae Based on Lactose Fermentation:

 

  • Lactose fermenters (pink colonies on MacConkey agar):
    Mnemonic: C-E-E-K (CHEEK)
    • Citrobacter
    • Enterobacter
    • E. coli
    • Klebsiella
  • Non-lactose fermenters (yellow colonies):
    • Proteus, Salmonella, Shigella (except Shigella sonnei), etc.
  • Late lactose fermenter (initially yellow, later pink):
    • Shigella sonnei

 

Other Options:

 

Option B. E. coli: E. coli also forms pink colonies (lactose-fermenting) but does not form mucoid colonies. It typically causes UTIs and diarrheal diseases, not necrotic pneumonia.

 

Option C. Moraxella catarrhalis: A non-lactose fermenter, associated with otitis media, bronchitis, and upper respiratory infections, not necrotizing pneumonia.

 

Option D. Burkholderia: Burkholderia is a non-lactose fermenter and does not produce mucoid colonies. It is associated with chronic lung infections, especially in cystic fibrosis.

 

Educational Objective:

 

Klebsiella pneumoniae is a lactose-fermenting, mucoid colony-forming bacterium that causes necrotizing pneumonia, commonly seen in chronic alcoholics and produces thick, sticky colonies due to its polysaccharide capsule.

questions.stem: The following is false about Adenovirus:

options.label: C
options.text: Hemorrhagic cystitis is due to type 11,21

questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. A) ssDNA virus

 

Adenovirus is a double-stranded DNA (dsDNA) virus. The statement that it is a single-stranded DNA (ssDNA) virus is false.

 

Key Characteristics of Adenovirus:

 

  • Genome: Double-stranded DNA (dsDNA) virus.
  • Capsid Shape: Icosahedral, non-enveloped (naked) virus.
  • Number of Serotypes: Over 53 serotypes.
  • Transmission: Spread by respiratory droplets, fecal-oral route, and direct contact.

 

Clinical Syndromes Caused by Adenovirus (by serotype):

 

  • Hemorrhagic cystitis: Caused by type 11 and 21. Presents with painful urination and hematuria (commonly seen in children and immunocompromised individuals).
  • Diarrhea: Caused by type 40 and 41. Commonly associated with pediatric gastroenteritis.
  • Pharyngoconjunctival fever: Caused by type 3, 4, 7. Presents with fever, pharyngitis, and conjunctivitis (common in military recruits).
  • Keratoconjunctivitis: Caused by type 8, 19, 37. Highly contagious epidemic eye infection.

 

Other Options:

 

Option B. Icosahedral: Correct. Adenovirus has an icosahedral capsid structure.

 

Option C. Hemorrhagic cystitis is due to type 11, 21: Correct. These serotypes cause hemorrhagic cystitis.

 

Option D. Diarrheagenic is due to type 40: Correct. Serotype 40 and 41 cause gastroenteritis, particularly in young children.

 

Educational Objective:

 

Adenovirus is a double-stranded DNA virus, not single-stranded (ssDNA). It has an icosahedral capsid, and specific serotypes cause distinct syndromes like hemorrhagic cystitis (types 11, 21) and diarrhea (type 40).

questions.stemHtml: Identify the organism from its egg in the picture?
questions.solutionHtml:
ize:14.0pt;">The explanation provides a helpful mnemonic "NEHA" to remember the transparent eggs:

 

  • N – Necator americanus (Hookworm)
  • E – Enterobius vermicularis
  • H – Hymenolepis nana
  • A – Ancylostoma duodenale (Hookworm)

 

The other important clue is the number of blastomeres. Hookworm eggs typically have four blastomeres at this stage of development.

 

Other Options:

 

Option A. Enterobius vermicularis: The eggs of Enterobius vermicularis (pinworm) are oval-shaped, flattened on one side, and contain a developing larva, not blastomeres. They are also typically yellow due to bile staining.

 

Option B. Trichuris trichiura: Trichuris trichiura (whipworm) eggs are barrel-shaped with characteristic bipolar plugs at each end. They are also yellow due to bile staining.

 

Option C. Ascaris lumbricoides: Ascaris lumbricoides (roundworm) eggs are typically round or oval with a thick outer shell that can be mammillated (covered in bumps). They are also yellow due to bile staining.

 

Educational Objective:

 

  • Hookworm eggs (Necator americanus and Ancylostoma duodenale) are transparent and typically contain four blastomeres.

questions.stem: In HIV window period indicates:

options.label: A
options.text: Time period between infection and onset of first symptoms

options.label: B
options.text: Time period between infection and detection of antibodies against HIV

options.label: C
options.text: Time period between infection and minimum multiplication of the organism

options.label: D
options.text: Time period between infection and maximum multiplication of the organism

questions.answerText: Time period between infection and detection of antibodies against HIV
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. B) Time period between infection and detection of antibodies against HIV

 

The window period in the context of HIV infection refers to the time between when a person is infected with the virus and when antibodies against HIV can be detected in the blood. When the HIV virus enters the human body through routes like sexual contact, blood transfusion, or needle sharing, the virus begins to multiply. However, it takes some time (typically 2 to 8 weeks) for the immune system to produce detectable antibodies (such as IgM and IgG) in response to the infection. During this period, even though the person is infected and the virus is present in their system, tests like ELISA and Western blot, which detect antibodies, may return a false-negative result. Therefore, diagnosing HIV during this period can be challenging.

 

To accurately diagnose HIV during the window period, tests that detect viral components (such as p24 antigen, a protein found on the HIV virus) are required, as they can detect the presence of the virus even before antibodies are formed.

 

Other Options:

 

Option A. Time period between infection and onset of first symptoms: Incorrect. The window period is unrelated to the onset of symptoms. HIV infection can remain asymptomatic for a long time after the window period.

 

Option C. Time period between infection and minimum multiplication of the organism: Incorrect. The window period does not refer to the viral replication level; instead, it focuses on the detection of antibodies.

 

Option D. Time period between infection and maximum multiplication of the organism: Incorrect. The virus multiplies rapidly after infection, but the window period pertains to the detection of antibodies, not viral load.

 

Educational Objective:

 

The window period is the time between HIV infection and the formation of detectable antibodies in the blood. During this time, antibody-based tests may yield negative results despite the presence of the virus, necessitating the use of tests that detect viral proteins like p24 antigen for early diagnosis.
