questions.stem: Pig tapeworm may cause dangerous disease than beef tapeworm because:
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. B) CNS involvement

 

Pig tapeworm, also known as Taenia solium, is more dangerous than beef tapeworm (Taenia saginata) because it can cause a condition known as neurocysticercosis. When a person ingests eggs of Taenia solium, rather than the larva from undercooked pork, the eggs hatch in the intestine and release larvae that can penetrate the intestinal wall, enter the bloodstream, and migrate to various organs, including the central nervous system (CNS). Once in the CNS, they form cysts, leading to neurocysticercosis, which can cause seizures, headaches, and other neurological complications. This CNS involvement makes Taenia solium significantly more dangerous.

 

In contrast, Taenia saginata, the beef tapeworm, only causes a gastrointestinal infection called taeniasis, which typically results in mild symptoms such as diarrhea, and does not involve the CNS.

 

Other Options:

 

Option A. Invasion of deep mucosa: Incorrect. The tapeworms do not invade the deep mucosa; they remain in the intestinal lumen.

 

Option C. Larger size: Incorrect. While Taenia saginata (beef tapeworm) is actually larger in size than Taenia solium, size does not correlate with the severity of disease. The pathogenicity depends on the life cycle and migration of the larvae, not the size of the adult tapeworm.

 

Option D. Eggs not infective to humans: Incorrect. The eggs of Taenia solium are indeed infective to humans, which is the primary reason for the danger associated with Taenia solium infections. If the eggs are ingested, they can lead to larval migration and cause systemic infection, unlike Taenia saginata.

 

Note:

 

Difference Between Taenia saginata (Beef Tapeworm) and Taenia solium (Pork Tapeworm)

 

 

Educational Objective:

 

Taenia solium (pork tapeworm) can cause neurocysticercosis due to the migration of larvae to the CNS after ingestion of eggs, making it more dangerous than Taenia saginata (beef tapeworm), which primarily causes intestinal taeniasis without systemic complications.

questions.stem: A 25-year-old female complains of recurrent rhinitis, nasal discharge and bilateral nasal blockage since 2 years. She has history of asthma and allergy. On examination multiple ethmoidal polyps are noted with mucosal thickening and impacted secretions in both the nasal cavities. Biopsy is taken and the material is cultured which shown the growth of many hyphae and pseudhohyphae with dichotomous branching typically at 45. Which of the following is the most likely responsible organism?
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. A) Aspergillus fumigatus

 

The clinical presentation of recurrent rhinitis, nasal polyps, and nasal blockage in a patient with a history of asthma and allergies is suggestive of allergic fungal rhinosinusitis (AFRS). The key diagnostic clue here is the presence of hyphae and pseudohyphae with dichotomous (branching) angles at 45°, which is characteristic of Aspergillus species, particularly Aspergillus fumigatus.

 

 

  • Aspergillus fumigatus has narrow, septate hyphae that branch dichotomously at acute angles (approximately 45°).
  • AFRS is commonly associated with Aspergillus species due to their ability to colonize mucus in the nasal cavities of immunocompromised or allergic patients.

 

The history of asthma and allergic reactions supports a hypersensitivity response that is commonly associated with Aspergillus infections.

 

Other Options:

 

Option B. Rhizopus:

 

  • Rhizopus is a type of fungus associated with mucormycosis, a more invasive and rapidly progressing infection seen typically in immunocompromised individuals, particularly those with diabetes mellitus or ketoacidosis.
  • Rhizopus forms broad, ribbon-like, aseptate hyphae with right-angle (90°) branching rather than the narrow, acute angles seen with Aspergillus.

 

 

Option C. Mucor:

 

  • Similar to Rhizopus, Mucor belongs to the Zygomycetes class and forms broad, non-septate hyphae with 90° branching.
  • Mucormycosis often presents with rapid tissue necrosis and can lead to significant facial and orbital destruction, which is different from the chronic presentation described in this case.

 

Option D. Candida:

 

  • Candida species typically cause yeast infections and form budding yeast cells with pseudohyphae rather than true hyphae.
  • Candida is not commonly associated with invasive or allergic fungal sinusitis and does not produce the characteristic dichotomous branching pattern seen at 45°.

 

Educational Objective:

 

The presence of narrow, septate hyphae with acute (45°) dichotomous branching is a hallmark feature of Aspergillus infections, distinguishing it from Zygomycetes (such as Rhizopus and Mucor), which have broad, aseptate hyphae with right-angle branching (90°).

questions.stem: A person presents with pneumonia. His sputum was sent for culture. The bacterium obtained was gram positive cocci in chains and alpha haemolytic colonies on sheep agar. Which of the following will help in confirming the diagnosis?
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. B) Optochin

 

The question describes gram-positive cocci in chains with alpha-hemolysis on blood agar, pointing towards Streptococcus species. Alpha-hemolysis (partial hemolysis) appears as a greenish discoloration around the colonies. The two primary alpha-hemolytic streptococci are Streptococcus pneumoniae and Streptococcus viridans. Since the clinical presentation involves pneumonia, Streptococcus pneumoniae is the likely pathogen, as viridans group streptococci typically cause endocarditis, not pneumonia.

 

The optochin sensitivity test helps distinguish Streptococcus pneumoniae from viridans group streptococci. Streptococcus pneumoniae is optochin-sensitive, meaning its growth is inhibited around an optochin disk, whereas viridans streptococci are resistant.

 

NOTE:

 

 

Other Options:

 

Option A. Novobiocin: This test is used to differentiate Staphylococcus saprophyticus (resistant) from Staphylococcus epidermidis (sensitive), not Streptococcus species.

 

Option C. Bacitracin: Bacitracin sensitivity is used to differentiate Streptococcus pyogenes (Group A Streptococcus) (sensitive) from other beta-hemolytic streptococci. It is not relevant for alpha-hemolytic streptococci.

 

Option D. Oxacillin: Oxacillin is an antibiotic used in determining methicillin resistance in Staphylococcus aureus, not in differentiating between species of Streptococcus.

 

Educational Objective:

 

Streptococcus pneumoniae is identified by its gram-positive cocci in chains, alpha-hemolytic colonies, and sensitivity to optochin, distinguishing it from viridans group streptococci, which are optochin-resistant.

questions.stem: Terminal spined eggs are seen in:
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. A) Schistosoma haematobium

 

Schistosoma haematobium is associated with urinary schistosomiasis, leading to hematuria (blood in urine), and the presence of terminal spined eggs in the urine is a hallmark diagnostic feature.

 

 

Other Options:

 

Option B. Schistosoma mansoni: Schistosoma mansoni eggs have a lateral spine, not a terminal spine. This species is associated with intestinal schistosomiasis and is endemic in Africa and South America.

 

 

Option C. Schistosoma japonicum: Schistosoma japonicum eggs have a small knob rather than a spine. This species also causes intestinal schistosomiasis and is commonly found in East Asia, particularly in regions like Japan and China.

 

 

Option D. Clonorchis sinensis: Clonorchis sinensis eggs are operculated (with a cap-like structure) and lack any spines. This parasite is known for causing liver fluke infections and is associated with biliary obstruction and cholangitis.

 

Educational Objective:

 

Terminal spined eggs are characteristic of Schistosoma haematobium, which causes urinary schistosomiasis and is detected through urine examination.

questions.stem: A rose gardener has multiple vesicles on hand and multiple eruptions along the lymphatics. Most common fungus responsible is:
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. A) Sporothrix schenckii

 

The clinical presentation describes a thorn prick followed by the development of nodules and vesicles along the lymphatic channels, which is a hallmark feature of sporotrichosis.

 

 

  • Sporotrichosis is a subcutaneous fungal infection caused by Sporothrix schenckii, a dimorphic fungus.
  • It is commonly known as “rose gardener’s disease” because it typically follows trauma caused by a thorn prick or a similar injury.
  • The infection spreads along the lymphatics, forming a "chain" of nodular lesions that may ulcerate.
  • A biopsy of the lesion often shows asteroid bodies or cigar-shaped yeast cells, which are diagnostic for Sporothrix schenckii.

 

 

Other Options:

 

Option B. Cladosporium: Cladosporium is associated with chromoblastomycosis, which presents as verrucous (warty) plaques rather than linear nodular eruptions along the lymphatics. It does not have a clear association with thorn pricks.

 

Option C. Histoplasma: Histoplasma capsulatum causes histoplasmosis, which is a systemic fungal infection primarily affecting the lungs. It is not typically associated with subcutaneous or lymphatic spread after skin trauma.

 

Option D. Candida: Candida species cause candidiasis, which usually presents as mucocutaneous or systemic infections. Candida is not known to cause lymphocutaneous spread or vesicles after a thorn prick.

 

Educational Objective:

 

Sporotrichosis, also known as "rose gardener’s disease," is caused by Sporothrix schenckii and presents as nodules and ulcers spreading along the lymphatics following trauma such as a thorn prick.

questions.stem: False about mechanism of bacterial toxins:

options.label: A
options.text: Cholera toxin acts by inhibition of guanylcyclase

options.label: C
options.text: Shiga toxin act by inhibiting protein synthesis

options.label: D
options.text: Diphtheria toxin act by inhibiting protein synthesis

questions.answerText: Cholera toxin acts by inhibition of guanylcyclase
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. A) Cholera toxin acts by inhibition of guanylcyclase

 

The mechanism of action of Cholera toxin involves activation of adenyl cyclase, not inhibition of guanylyl cyclase. The toxin enters intestinal epithelial cells and activates adenyl cyclase, leading to increased production of cyclic AMP (cAMP). This results in massive ion efflux and water secretion into the intestinal lumen, causing severe watery diarrhea (rice water stools).

 

Other Options:

 

Option B. Botulinum toxin inhibits Ach release: True. Botulinum toxin inhibits the release of acetylcholine, preventing muscle contraction, which causes flaccid paralysis.

 

Option C. Shiga toxin acts by inhibiting protein synthesis: True. Shiga toxin inhibits protein synthesis by targeting the 60S ribosomal subunit, leading to cell death.

 

Option D. Diphtheria toxin acts by inhibiting protein synthesis: True. Diphtheria toxin inactivates elongation factor-2 (EF-2), blocking protein synthesis and causing cell death.

 

NOTE:

 

 

Educational Objective:

 

Cholera toxin does not inhibit guanylyl cyclase; it activates adenyl cyclase, leading to increased cAMP and watery diarrhea.

questions.stem: True about antigenic drift:

options.label: D
options.text: Arises due to frame shift mutations

questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. B) Leads to seasonal epidemics

 

Antigenic drift is a mechanism of genetic variation that occurs gradually over time due to point mutations in the genes encoding the hemagglutinin (H) and neuraminidase (N) surface proteins of the influenza virus. This gradual accumulation of mutations allows the virus to evade the immune response, as the antibodies generated from previous infections or vaccinations may no longer fully recognize the mutated virus.

 

Key features of antigenic drift:

 

  • It occurs in influenza A and B viruses.
  • It results in seasonal epidemics (localized outbreaks).
  • It is caused by point mutations, not frameshift mutations.
  • Since the changes are minor and gradual, the new virus is partially related to the parent strain, meaning some immunity may still exist.

 

In contrast, antigenic shift is a sudden, major change in the virus due to the reassortment of genetic material between different influenza A viruses. This results in the emergence of a novel virus that can lead to pandemics because the population lacks immunity against it.

 

 

Other Options:

 

Option A. Caused only by influenza A: False. Antigenic drift occurs in both influenza A and B viruses. However, antigenic shift occurs only in influenza A, which has a broader host range, including humans, birds, and pigs.

 

Option C. Leads to pandemic: False. Pandemics are caused by antigenic shift, not antigenic drift. Antigenic shift produces a completely new strain due to reassortment of viral RNA segments, which can spread globally.

 

Option D. Arises due to frameshift mutations: False. Antigenic drift is caused by point mutations in the genetic code, not frameshift mutations (which are insertions or deletions of nucleotides that change the reading frame).

 

Educational Objective:

 

Antigenic drift refers to the gradual accumulation of point mutations in influenza A and B, leading to seasonal epidemics rather than pandemics.

questions.stem: An army jawan posted in remote forest area following a tick bite had fever and headache. His fever was 104 °F and pulse was 70 per min. He had an erythematous lesion of about 1 cm on the leg surrounded by small vesicles, along with generalized lymphadenopathy at the time of presentation to the referral hospital. His blood sample was collected to perform serology for the diagnosis of Rickettsial disease. Which one of the following results in Weil-Felix reaction will be diagnostic in this clinical setting?
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. D) High OX – 19 and OX – 2

 

The clinical presentation of tick bite, fever, and vesicular lesions along with lymphadenopathy strongly suggests Rickettsial infection, most likely Indian Tick Typhus (Spotted Fever Group) or Rocky Mountain Spotted Fever (RMSF). These infections are caused by Rickettsia rickettsii or Rickettsia conorii and are transmitted by ticks.

 

The Weil-Felix reaction is a diagnostic agglutination test based on cross-reacting antigens of Proteus strains (OX-19, OX-2, OX-K). The antigens detected for specific Rickettsial diseases are as follows:

 

  • OX-19: Positive in epidemic and endemic typhus, spotted fever group
  • OX-2: Positive in the spotted fever group (e.g., Indian Tick Typhus, RMSF)
  • OX-K: Positive in scrub typhus (Orientia tsutsugamushi)

 

In the spotted fever group (e.g., RMSF, Indian tick typhus), both OX-19 and OX-2 are positive, making this the diagnostic result.

 

Other Options:

 

Option A. High OX-2: In the Weil-Felix reaction, OX-2 is not detected in isolation; it is positive alongside OX-19 in spotted fever infections.

 

Option B. High OX-19: OX-19 alone is associated with epidemic typhus (R. prowazekii) and endemic typhus (R. typhi), not with tick-borne Rickettsial diseases like RMSF or Indian Tick Typhus.

 

Option C. High OX-K: OX-K is specific for scrub typhus (Orientia tsutsugamushi) and is not seen in spotted fever or typhus.

 

Additional information:

 

 

Educational Objective:

 

In cases of spotted fever Rickettsial diseases (e.g., Indian tick typhus and RMSF), the Weil-Felix reaction shows positivity for both OX-19 and OX-2. Conversely, OX-K positivity is indicative of scrub typhus.

questions.stem: EBV receptors is:
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. A) CD 21

 

Epstein-Barr Virus (EBV), also known as the “kissing virus,” is a herpesvirus that spreads primarily through saliva. Once EBV enters the body, it targets B lymphocytes by binding to a specific surface receptor known as CD 21, which is also known as the C3d complement receptor. This receptor is present on B cells and some epithelial cells of the nasopharynx.

 

 

After binding to CD 21, EBV can enter the B cells, where it establishes either a latent infection or an active lytic infection. EBV infection is associated with conditions such as:

 

  • Infectious mononucleosis (primary infection)

 

 

  • Burkitt lymphoma (oncogenesis in B cells)
  • Nasopharyngeal carcinoma
  • Post-transplant lymphoproliferative disorder (PTLD)

 

Other Options:

 

Option B. CD 9: CD 9 is associated with cell adhesion and signaling processes but has no role in EBV attachment.

 

Option C. CD 10: CD 10 is a marker of early B cell precursors and is used as a diagnostic marker in B-cell lymphomas and acute lymphoblastic leukemia (ALL), but it is not involved in EBV infection.

 

Option D. CD 8: CD 8 is a marker for cytotoxic T lymphocytes (CTLs), which play a role in the immune response to EBV-infected cells but are not used as an EBV receptor.

 

Educational Objective:

 

Epstein-Barr Virus (EBV) uses the CD 21 receptor on B lymphocytes to enter the cell, making it a key step in its pathogenesis and oncogenic potential.

questions.stemHtml: A patient presented with complaints of dysphagia. On UGI Endoscopy a diagnosis of esophageal candidiasis was made. The organism obtained from the sample was cultured on a specialized media and the below finding were visible on microscopy of the culture. What phenomenon is shown below?
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. A) Germ tube formation

 

The diagnosis of esophageal candidiasis indicates the involvement of Candida species, most commonly Candida albicans. The microscopic image shows elongated filamentous projections extending from the yeast cells, characteristic of germ tube formation.

 

The germ tube test is a rapid method used to identify Candida albicans from other Candida species:

 

  • A sample containing the yeast is incubated in human serum at 37°C for 2–3 hours.
  • If the organism is Candida albicans, germ tubes (tube-like extensions) form from the yeast cells.
  • This phenomenon is also known as the Reynolds-Braude phenomenon.

 

Other Options:

 

Option B. Spore formation: Candida albicans can form chlamydospores on cornmeal agar during specific tests, but these are spherical, not elongated germ tubes.

 

Option C. Mould to yeast formation: This is a phenomenon seen in dimorphic fungi such as Histoplasma or Blastomyces, not Candida species. Candida does not show dimorphic transitions involving mould and yeast forms.

 

Option D. Budding: Budding refers to the asexual reproduction of yeast cells, where a small daughter cell buds off from the mother cell. Budding produces rounded structures, not the filamentous germ tubes seen in the image.

 

Educational Objective:

 

Germ tube formation is the hallmark test for the identification of Candida albicans and is not seen in other Candida species. It involves the formation of filamentous extensions in the presence of human serum.

questions.stem: In patient with Malaria, if fever has periodicity of 72 hours, which one of the following is likely to be causative agent?
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. D) P. Malariae

 

In malaria, the periodicity of fever corresponds to the erythrocytic cycle (the time taken by the parasite to complete its life cycle in red blood cells). The duration of the fever cycle is different for each Plasmodium species:

 

  • P. vivax and P. ovale: Fever occurs every 48 hours (tertian fever).
  • P. falciparum: Fever is irregular but often appears every 48 hours in classic cases.
  • P. malariae: Fever occurs every 72 hours (quartan fever).

 

In P. malariae infection, the fever pattern is described as quartan fever because it recurs on the fourth day (i.e., after an interval of 72 hours).

 

Educational Objective:

 

P. malariae is the only Plasmodium species that produces a 72-hour fever cycle (quartan fever), distinguishing it from other species that typically cause 48-hour fever cycles (tertian fever).

questions.stem: An HIV+ve patient with CD4 Count 20 cells/mm3 came with complaints of headache, mild neck stiffness and weakness suspected Meningitis, lumbar puncture revealed yeast with no pseudohyphae. India ink preparation shows capsule. Diagnosis:
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. B) Cryptococcus

 

In an HIV-positive patient with severe immunosuppression (CD4 count <200 cells/mm³), opportunistic infections are common. Meningitis in this setting is often caused by Cryptococcus neoformans, a capsulated yeast that is detected using India ink staining.

 

 

  • Cryptococcus neoformans is a yeast that does not form pseudohyphae and is unique for its polysaccharide capsule. The India ink preparation demonstrates this capsule as a clear halo around the yeast cells against a dark background.
  • The capsule is an important virulence factor that helps the organism evade phagocytosis.
  • Cryptococcal meningitis presents with headache, fever, neck stiffness, and altered mental status, particularly in severely immunocompromised patients (e.g., those with HIV/AIDS and low CD4 counts).

 

Other Options:

 

Option A. Candida: Candida species form pseudohyphae in tissue and do not have a capsule. While Candida can cause meningitis, it is rare and typically occurs in patients with indwelling devices or recent surgeries.

 

Option C. Aspergillus: Aspergillus is a mold that forms septate hyphae and typically causes pulmonary infections rather than meningitis. It does not produce a capsule.

 

Option D. Mucor: Mucor species are also molds, forming broad, aseptate hyphae with 90° branching. Mucormycosis typically causes rhinocerebral infections in diabetic or immunosuppressed patients but does not present as encapsulated yeast on India ink preparation.

 

Educational Objective:

 

Cryptococcus neoformans is a capsulated yeast that is identified using India ink staining and commonly causes cryptococcal meningitis in HIV-positive patients with low CD4 counts.

questions.stem: Which is the first antibody synthesised in fetal life?
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. B) IgM

 

There are five types of antibodies: IgG, IgA, IgM, IgD, and IgE (mnemonic: GAMDE). 

 

In fetal life, antibody synthesis begins around the 20th week of gestation.

 

  • The first antibody synthesized by the fetus is IgM. This is an indication of the fetus's ability to mount its own immune response.
  • The fetus cannot produce IgG initially—IgG in the fetal circulation comes from the mother. IgG is the only antibody that can cross the placenta and provides passive immunity to the fetus.

 

Other Options:

 

Option A. IgA: IgA is primarily found in secretions (e.g., saliva, breast milk, mucosal surfaces) and is produced later in life after birth.

 

Option C. IgG: IgG is the first antibody present in fetal circulation due to passive transfer from the mother but is not synthesized by the fetus.

 

Option D. IgE: IgE is associated with allergic reactions and parasitic infections and is not synthesized in significant quantities during fetal life.

 

Educational Objective:

 

The first antibody synthesized by the fetus is IgM (from around the 20th week of gestation), while the first antibody present in the fetal circulation is IgG, passively transferred from the mother.

questions.stem: A child with bull neck and membrane over tonsil. What is mechanism of the toxin responsible for this condition?
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. C) Inhibits Elongation Factor-2

 

The clinical presentation of bull neck (enlarged cervical lymph nodes) and pseudomembrane formation over the tonsils is characteristic of diphtheria, caused by Corynebacterium diphtheriae.

 

  • The diphtheria toxin is an exotoxin that inhibits protein synthesis by ADP-ribosylating elongation factor-2 (EF-2).
  • EF-2 is essential for the elongation step during mRNA translation in protein synthesis.
  • Inhibition of EF-2 leads to cell death, particularly affecting epithelial cells in the upper respiratory tract and causing the formation of a thick pseudomembrane.
  • Systemic spread of the toxin can lead to myocarditis, neuropathy, and multiorgan failure.

 

The mnemonic “Delhi Public Secondary School” helps to recall that toxins from Diphtheria, Pseudomonas, Shiga, and Shiga-like toxins all inhibit EF-2.

 

Other Options:

 

Option A. Increased cAMP: Toxins that increase cAMP levels (via adenyl cyclase activation) include:

 

  • Bacillus anthracis (edema factor)
  • Bordetella pertussis (pertussis toxin)
  • Vibrio cholerae (cholera toxin)
  • ETEC

 

Option B. Inhibits GABA neurons: Clostridium tetani releases tetanospasmin, which inhibits the release of GABA and glycine from inhibitory neurons, leading to spastic paralysis.

 

Option D. Inhibits release of acetylcholine: Clostridium botulinum produces botulinum toxin, which inhibits the release of acetylcholine at the neuromuscular junction, causing flaccid paralysis.

 

Educational Objective:

 

The diphtheria toxin inhibits protein synthesis by ADP-ribosylation of elongation factor-2 (EF-2), leading to cell death, which manifests as a pseudomembrane and bull neck in diphtheria.

questions.stemHtml: Women presented with dome-shaped warty lesions with a dimple at center on forehead since 2 months, similar lesions noticed in her daughter (image given) causative agent?
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. A) Poxvirus 

 

The clinical presentation and image show umbilicated (dimpled) dome-shaped papules, which are characteristic of molluscum contagiosum. This condition is caused by the Molluscum contagiosum virus (MCV), which belongs to the Poxvirus family.

 

  • Molluscum contagiosum presents as multiple, discrete, dome-shaped, flesh-colored papules with a central umbilication (dimple).
  • The lesions are highly contagious and can spread through direct contact, which explains why similar lesions are present in the daughter.
  • The condition is benign and self-limiting but can persist for months if untreated.

 

Other Options:

 

Option B. Human Herpesvirus 6 (HHV-6): HHV-6 is associated with roseola infantum (exanthem subitum), which presents as a maculopapular rash following a high fever, not with umbilicated lesions.

 

Option C. Papillomavirus: Human papillomavirus (HPV) causes common warts, plantar warts, and genital warts. These lesions are typically hyperkeratotic and do not show a central dimple or umbilication.

 

Option D. Coxsackie virus: Coxsackie virus causes hand-foot-and-mouth disease and herpangina. The associated lesions are vesicular, not umbilicated.

 

Educational Objective:

 

Molluscum contagiosum presents with dome-shaped, umbilicated lesions caused by the Poxvirus family. The hallmark feature is the central dimple in each lesion, making it a distinct clinical diagnosis.

questions.stem: A person working in an abattoir presented with a pustule on his hand that progressed to form an ulcer. Smear is taken from the ulcer and sent to laboratory for investigation. Which of the following is the best stain to determine the causative agent of the ulcer?
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. A) Trichrome methylene blue

 

The clinical scenario points towards cutaneous anthrax, which is caused by Bacillus anthracis, a zoonotic pathogen commonly associated with abattoir workers, butchers, and farmers. The disease begins as a pustule that progresses into a necrotic ulcer with a central eschar ("malignant pustule").

 

 

The McFadyean reaction is the diagnostic method for Bacillus anthracis, which involves staining the sample with methylene blue. When viewed under the microscope, this stain demonstrates:

 

  • Purple-blue bacilli with a surrounding pink-stained capsule (due to the capsule composed of poly-D-glutamic acid).

 

This distinctive appearance is crucial for identifying Bacillus anthracis in clinical samples.

 

Other Options:

 

Option B. Carbol fuchsin: Carbol fuchsin is used in Ziehl-Neelsen staining for identifying acid-fast bacilli (e.g., Mycobacterium tuberculosis). Bacillus anthracis is not acid-fast.

 

Option C. Acid-fast stain: Acid-fast stains (like Ziehl-Neelsen or Kinyoun) are specific for organisms like Mycobacterium and Nocardia but not effective for Bacillus anthracis.

 

Option D. Calcofluor white: Calcofluor white is a fluorescent stain used for identifying fungal elements by binding to chitin and cellulose in fungal cell walls. It is not applicable for bacteria like Bacillus anthracis.

 

Educational Objective:

 

The McFadyean reaction (using methylene blue stain) is the best method for identifying Bacillus anthracis, showing purple-blue bacilli with a pink capsule. The clinical clue of working in an abattoir and presenting with a cutaneous ulcer points strongly to cutaneous anthrax.

questions.stem: A hospital worker is found to be HBsAg (+) ve. Further serum investigations showed HBe (+) ve and IgG anti HBc (+) ve. The given hospital worker is:

options.label: A
options.text: Acute Hepatitis B patient with High infectivity

questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. C) Chronic infection with high infectivity

 

The serological markers in Hepatitis B infection help distinguish between different phases of the disease. 

 

Let’s break down the findings:

 

  • HBsAg (+) (Hepatitis B surface antigen): Indicates active infection (whether acute or chronic).
  • HBeAg (+) (Hepatitis B envelope antigen): Indicates high viral replication and high infectivity.
  • Anti-HBc IgG (+) (IgG antibody against core antigen): Indicates a chronic infection because IgG suggests long-standing infection (whereas IgM would indicate acute infection).

 

Other Options:

 

Option A. Acute Hepatitis B patient with high infectivity: Acute infection would be indicated by anti-HBc IgM instead of IgG.

 

Option B. Simple carrier with high infectivity: A carrier usually has low or no HBeAg (low infectivity) and typically no evidence of active replication. This patient has active viral replication, as shown by HBeAg (+).

 

Option D. Immunized person for Hepatitis B: An immunized person would have anti-HBs antibodies (indicating immunity) and no HBsAg or anti-HBc (since the vaccine does not contain the core antigen).

 

Educational Objective:

 

In chronic Hepatitis B infection, HBsAg remains positive for more than 6 months, anti-HBc IgG is positive, and HBeAg positivity indicates high viral replication and high infectivity.

questions.stem: Which of the following is ovo-viviparous?
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. A) Strongyloidis stercoralis

 

Ovoviviparous organisms produce eggs that hatch inside the body, and they release larvae rather than eggs.

 

 Strongyloides stercoralis is unique in being ovoviviparous.

 

  • Females produce larvae, not eggs, making it ovoviviparous.
  • The larvae hatch inside the host and are released as rhabditiform larvae in the stool.

 

Other options:

 

Option B. Trichinella spiralis: Trichinella spiralis is viviparous, meaning it gives birth to live larvae.

 

Option C. Enterobius (pinworm): Oviparous, meaning it lays eggs directly into the environment.

 

Option D. Ascaris lumbricoides (roundworm): Oviparous, meaning it releases eggs that hatch outside the host.

 

Educational Objective:

 

Strongyloides stercoralis is ovoviviparous (produces larvae instead of eggs), while other nematodes such as Ascaris, Enterobius, and Trichinella follow different reproductive methods.

questions.stem: Fish acts as intermediate host in:
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. A) D. latum

 

Diphyllobothrium latum (D. latum) is a broad fish tapeworm and requires two intermediate hosts for its life cycle:

 

  1. Definitive host: Humans (sometimes other mammals like dogs, cats, bears).
  2. First intermediate host: Cyclops (a type of freshwater crustacean), where the coracidium larvae develop into procercoid larvae.
  3. Second intermediate host: Fish (such as freshwater species like pike, trout, and perch), where the procercoid larvae further develop into plerocercoid larvae, which are infective to humans.

 

Humans become infected by consuming raw or undercooked fish containing plerocercoid larvae. The adult worm resides in the intestines, causing diphyllobothriasis. The most common clinical symptoms are vague abdominal discomfort, vitamin B12 deficiency, and megaloblastic anemia.

 

Other Options:

 

Option B. E. granulosis: Echinococcus granulosus does not involve fish in its life cycle. Instead, its definitive host is dogs, while intermediate hosts are typically herbivorous mammals (e.g., sheep, cattle, or humans in hydatid disease).

 

Option C. H. diminuta: Hymenolepis diminuta uses grain beetles or fleas as intermediate hosts rather than fish. The definitive host is usually rodents, though humans can be accidental hosts.

 

Option D. H. nana: Hymenolepis nana (the dwarf tapeworm) is unique in that it does not require an intermediate host, although beetles can act as a host in some cases. Its direct transmission occurs via ingestion of contaminated food or water.

 

Educational Objective:

 

The fish tapeworm D. latum uses Cyclops as the first intermediate host and fish as the second intermediate host, while humans are the definitive host.

questions.stem: Which of the following is microaerophilic?
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. A) Campylobacter

 

Microaerophilic organisms require low levels of oxygen for survival, typically around 5% oxygen concentration, which is significantly lower than atmospheric oxygen levels (~21%). These bacteria thrive in environments with reduced oxygen levels.

 

The mnemonic "Help, Camp is Boring" helps to remember the main microaerophilic bacteria:

 

  • Help → Helicobacter pylori
  • Camp → Campylobacter
  • Boring → Borrelia

 

In this case, Campylobacter is the correct answer, as it grows best in environments with only 5% oxygen.

 

Other Options:

 

Option B. Vibrio: Vibrio species (e.g., Vibrio cholerae) are facultative anaerobes, meaning they can survive in both oxygen-rich and oxygen-poor conditions but do not require low oxygen levels like microaerophiles.

 

Option C. Bacteroides: Bacteroides species are strict anaerobes, meaning they cannot tolerate oxygen and grow only in oxygen-free environments.

 

Option D. Pseudomonas: Pseudomonas species (e.g., Pseudomonas aeruginosa) are aerobic bacteria, meaning they require oxygen for growth and thrive in oxygen-rich environments.

 

Educational Objective:

 

Microaerophilic bacteria, such as Campylobacter, Helicobacter pylori, and Borrelia, require only 5% oxygen for optimal growth. Use the mnemonic "Help, Camp is Boring" to remember these organisms.

questions.stem: Which of the following egg contains three pairs of hooklets and polar filaments but bile non stained?
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. A) H. Nana

 

Hymenolepis nana (commonly known as the dwarf tapeworm) produces bile non-stained, transparent eggs that have distinct features:

 

  • Color: Transparent (bile non-stained).
  • Hooklets: Contains three pairs of hooklets (six total) inside the egg.
  • Polar filaments: Present and seen radiating from the inner embryophore.

 

Bile staining refers to a characteristic yellowish tint that some helminth eggs acquire due to bile pigments. In contrast, H. nana eggs remain colorless and transparent, distinguishing them from bile-stained eggs of other tapeworm species.

 

Other Options:

 

Option B. T. solium: The eggs of Taenia solium (pork tapeworm) are bile-stained, round, and have a thick, radially striated shell with an oncosphere containing three pairs of hooklets but no polar filaments.

 

Option C. T. saginata: The eggs of Taenia saginata (beef tapeworm) are morphologically identical to T. solium eggs and are also bile-stained, round, and striated, with an oncosphere containing three pairs of hooklets but no polar filaments.

 

Option D. E. granulosus: The eggs of Echinococcus granulosus (hydatid tapeworm) resemble Taenia eggs—bile-stained, with a thick shell, radial striations, and three pairs of hooklets, but no polar filaments.

 

Educational Objective:

 

The eggs of Hymenolepis nana are bile non-stained (transparent) and have polar filaments and three pairs of hooklets. Other tapeworm eggs, such as Taenia and Echinococcus, are bile-stained and lack polar filaments. Use the mnemonic "Neha" to remember the bile non-stained eggs.

questions.stem: A woman with infertility receives an ovary transplant from her sister who is an identical twin. What type of graft is?
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. D) Isograft

 

A graft refers to the transplantation of tissues or organs from a donor to a recipient. The classification of grafts is based on the relationship between the donor and recipient.

 

 

  1. Autograft: Transplant from the same individual (self). Example: Skin graft from one part of the body to another in the same person (e.g., for burns).
  2. Isograft (Syngraft): Transplant between genetically identical individuals, such as identical twins. Since their genetic material (including human leukocyte antigens, HLA) is the same, the body does not reject the transplant.
  3. Allograft: Transplant between two genetically different individuals of the same species (e.g., one human to another human). These are the most common types of grafts and require immunosuppressants to prevent rejection.
  4. Xenograft: Transplant between different species (e.g., pig heart valves transplanted into humans). These have a high chance of rejection due to vast genetic differences.

 

In this case, since the donor is an identical twin, the graft is called an isograft, as there is a 100% genetic match, ensuring no immune rejection.

 

Other Options:

 

Option A. Xenograft: A transplant from an animal to a human (different species). Example: Pig heart valves used in cardiac surgeries. This option is incorrect in the context of an identical twin.

 

Option B. Autograft: A transplant where the donor and recipient are the same person. Example: Skin graft from thigh to arm. In this case, the donor is the sister, not the same person.

 

Option C. Allograft: A transplant between two genetically different humans (non-identical siblings or unrelated individuals). Since the donor is an identical twin, this option is incorrect.

 

Educational Objective:

 

An isograft is a transplant between genetically identical individuals, such as identical twins, making it the least likely to be rejected due to a perfect genetic match.

In this case, since the donor is an identical twin, the graft is called an isograft, as there is a 100% genetic match, ensuring no immune rejection. Other Options: Option A. Xenograft: A transplant from an animal to a human (different species). Example: Pig heart valves used in cardiac surgeries. This option is incorrect in the context of an identical twin. Option B. Autograft: A transplant where the donor and recipient are the same person. Example: Skin graft from thigh to arm. In this case, the donor is the sister, not the same person. Option C. Allograft: A transplant between two genetically different humans (non-identical siblings or unrelated individuals). Since the donor is an identical twin, this option is incorrect. Educational Objective: An isograft is a transplant between genetically identical individuals, such as identical twins, making it the least likely to be rejected due to a perfect genetic match.

questions.stem: There has been an outbreak of food born salmonella gastroenteritis in the community and the stool samples have been received in the laboratory. Which is the enrichment medium of choice?
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. C) Selenite ‘F’ medium

 

Enrichment media are used to favor the growth of a particular organism, especially when the pathogen is present in small numbers and can be overgrown by normal flora in the sample. In the case of Salmonella gastroenteritis, Selenite F medium is the enrichment medium of choice.

 

 

  • Selenite F medium:
    • Specifically designed to inhibit the growth of coliform bacteria (normal intestinal flora) while allowing the selective enrichment of Salmonella species.
    • It contains selenite, which is toxic to some Gram-positive and Gram-negative bacteria but permits Salmonella growth.
    • It is particularly useful for stool samples suspected of containing Salmonella.

 

This makes Selenite F medium an essential tool in outbreak investigations involving Salmonella infections.

 

Other Options:

 

Option A. Cary Blair medium: Cary Blair medium is a transport medium used to preserve stool specimens during transport to the lab. It prevents the overgrowth of bacteria during transit but is not an enrichment medium.

 

Option B. VR medium: VR (Violet Red) medium is used for the isolation of coliforms from food and water samples, not for the enrichment of Salmonella.

 

Option D. Thioglycollate medium: Thioglycollate medium is a general-purpose medium used to culture anaerobic bacteria. It is not selective for Salmonella and is therefore not suitable in this context.

 

Educational Objective:

 

For Salmonella enrichment, Selenite F medium is used to selectively allow the growth of Salmonella while inhibiting other competing bacteria, particularly coliforms, making it the ideal enrichment medium in outbreak investigations.

questions.stem: Patient is presented with cough with rusty sputum. On examination, lower lobe consolidation and bronchial breath sounds were heard. It gives a positive Quellung reaction. What is the probable Gram staining appearance?
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. B) Gram +ve cocci

 

The clinical presentation of pneumonia with rusty-colored sputum and positive Quellung reaction strongly suggests infection by Streptococcus pneumoniae.

 

  • Quellung reaction: A diagnostic test for detecting bacterial capsules. When specific antibodies bind to the capsule of Streptococcus pneumoniae, the capsule swells and becomes visible under the microscope, indicating a positive Quellung reaction.
  • Morphology of Streptococcus pneumoniae:
    • Gram stain appearance: Gram-positive cocci (purple-stained under Gram stain).
    • Shape: Lancet (flame)-shaped diplococci (pairs of cocci).
    • Capsule: Encapsulated, contributing to its virulence and visibility in the Quellung test.

 

Streptococcus pneumoniae is the most common cause of community-acquired pneumonia (CAP) and is associated with rust-colored sputum due to alveolar bleeding.

 

Other Options:

 

Option A. Gram-negative bacilli: Gram-negative bacilli (e.g., Klebsiella pneumoniae, Escherichia coli) can also cause pneumonia but do not give a positive Quellung reaction and typically appear rod-shaped.

 

Option C. Gram-positive bacilli: Gram-positive bacilli (e.g., Bacillus anthracis, Clostridium species) are rod-shaped and do not show a positive Quellung reaction.

 

Option D. Gram-negative diplococci: Gram-negative diplococci (e.g., Neisseria meningitidis, Moraxella catarrhalis) appear as paired, kidney-shaped diplococci but are not associated with a positive Quellung reaction or rusty sputum.

 

Educational Objective:

 

Streptococcus pneumoniae is a Gram-positive, flame-shaped diplococcus that causes pneumonia with rusty sputum and gives a positive Quellung reaction due to its capsule swelling in the presence of specific antibodies.

questions.stemHtml: Which is the mode of transmission and infective form of the parasite whose egg picture is given below?

options.label: B
options.text: Ingestion of egg contaminated in water

questions.answerText: Ingestion of egg contaminated in water
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. B) Ingestion of egg contaminated in water

 

The image shows the egg of Trichuris trichiura, commonly known as the whipworm. The characteristics of the egg include:

 

  • Shape: Barrel-shaped (lemon-shaped or football-shaped).
  • Color: Bile-stained (yellowish).
  • Ends: Has bipolar mucus plugs at each pole.

 

Trichuris trichiura causes trichuriasis, and the transmission occurs when a person ingests embryonated eggs from contaminated water or food. Once ingested, the eggs hatch in the intestine, and the larvae mature into adult worms.

 

Infective Form:

 

  • Embryonated eggs in contaminated food or water.

 

Mode of Transmission:

 

  • Fecal-oral route via ingestion of eggs present in contaminated water or food.

 

Other Options:

 

Option A. Ingestion of uncooked/raw beef: This is the mode of transmission for Taenia saginata (beef tapeworm), which is acquired by consuming raw or undercooked beef containing cysticerci (larval forms).

 

Option C. Penetration by filariform larva: This is the mode of transmission for Ancylostoma duodenale and Necator americanus (hookworms), where the filariform larvae penetrate the skin of the host, typically through the feet.

 

Option D. Penetration by rhabditiform larva: Rhabditiform larvae are the non-infective stage of Strongyloides stercoralis. The filariform larvae are the infective stage, not the rhabditiform larvae.

 

Educational Objective:

 

The characteristic barrel-shaped, bile-stained egg with bipolar plugs belongs to Trichuris trichiura. The mode of transmission is ingestion of embryonated eggs from contaminated water or food.

questions.stem: A 20-year-old male with history of fever and enlarged lymph nodes and sore throat was suspected to have infectious mononucleosis and was ordered a Paul Bunnel test. Which of the following is the principle of the test?
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. A) Heterophile agglutination test

 

The Paul Bunnell test is used to detect heterophile antibodies in the serum of patients suspected of having infectious mononucleosis (caused by the Epstein-Barr virus).

 

  • Heterophile antibodies: These are nonspecific antibodies that react with antigens from unrelated species.
  • In the Paul Bunnell test, sheep or horse erythrocytes are mixed with the patient’s serum. If heterophile antibodies are present, they cause agglutination (clumping of erythrocytes).

 

This test takes advantage of the fact that patients with infectious mononucleosis produce large amounts of heterophile antibodies, which can cross-react with red blood cells from other species.

 

Other Options:

 

Option B. Neutralization test: A test used to detect neutralizing antibodies that can prevent viral infection or neutralize a toxin. It is not relevant to the Paul Bunnell test.

 

Option C. Complement-mediated cell damage: This describes tests that involve complement proteins leading to cell lysis, such as complement fixation tests. The Paul Bunnell test does not involve complement activation.

 

Option D. Agglutination reaction: While agglutination is part of the test, it specifically involves heterophile antibodies reacting with erythrocytes from other species, making it a heterophile agglutination test rather than a simple agglutination reaction.

 

Educational Objective:

 

The Paul Bunnell test is based on the principle of heterophile agglutination, where heterophile antibodies present in the serum cause agglutination of sheep or horse red blood cells, indicating infectious mononucleosis due to the Epstein-Barr virus (EBV).

questions.stem: Ziemann dots:
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. C) Plasmodium malariae

 

  • Ziemann dots: Seen in Plasmodium malariae infections and appear as fine, dust-like granules in infected red blood cells.

 

 

Mnemonic:

 

"See Many Zebra in the Jungle"

 

  • S: Schüffner dots → P. vivax
  • M: Maurer dots → P. falciparum
  • Z: Ziemann dots → P. malariae
  • J: James dots → P. ovale

 

Or: "Very Fantastic Medical Officer"

 

  • V: Vivax → Schüffner
  • F: Falciparum → Maurer
  • M: Malariae → Ziemann
  • O: Ovale → James

 

Educational Objective:

 

Ziemann dots are a hallmark of Plasmodium malariae infections and appear as fine granules within the infected red blood cells. Remember the mnemonics to differentiate between the dots associated with different species of Plasmodium.

questions.stem: A 12-year-old child presents with fever and cervical lymphadenopathy. Oral examination shows a grey membrane on the right tonsil extending to the anterior pillar. Which of the following medium will be ideal for the culture of the throat swab for a rapid identification of the pathogen?
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. C) Loffler’s serum slope

 

The presence of a grey membrane over the tonsil with cervical lymphadenopathy in a child is highly indicative of diphtheria, an infection caused by Corynebacterium diphtheriae.

 

  • Löffler's serum slope:
    • An enrichment medium that enhances the growth of Corynebacterium diphtheriae by providing essential nutrients.
    • It contains serum, which promotes the production of metachromatic granules (seen as beaded structures within the bacilli).
    • Colonies appear quickly (within 6–8 hours) and can be rapidly identified microscopically by their characteristic club-shaped, beaded, Gram-positive bacilli.

 

In addition to Löffler’s medium, potassium tellurite agar (Hoyle’s medium) is a selective medium for the isolation of C. diphtheriae and shows black-colored colonies.

 

Other Options:

 

Option A. Nutrient agar: A basic medium used for non-fastidious bacteria. It is not suitable for rapid or selective growth of Corynebacterium diphtheriae.

 

Option B. Blood agar: While useful for growing many bacteria, Corynebacterium diphtheriae requires a more enriched medium for rapid detection, such as Löffler’s medium.

 

Option D. Lowenstein-Jensen (LJ) medium: A selective medium used for Mycobacterium tuberculosis. It is irrelevant in the case of diphtheria.

 

Educational Objective:

 

For rapid identification of diphtheria, Löffler’s serum slope is the enrichment medium of choice, facilitating the observation of characteristic metachromatic granules in Corynebacterium diphtheriae. Additionally, potassium tellurite agar can be used to detect black colonies.

questions.stem: All are true about Chagas’ disease except:

options.label: A
options.text: Romana's sign is a diagnostic feature of acute Chagas’ disease

options.label: B
options.text: Tsetse fly is the vector (Glossina palpalis)

questions.answerText: Tsetse fly is the vector (Glossina palpalis)
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. B) Tsetse fly is the vector (Glossina palpalis)

 

Chagas’ disease is caused by Trypanosoma cruzi and is transmitted by Reduviid bugs (also known as kissing bugs). The following are the characteristic features of Chagas’ disease:

 

  • Vector: The vector is the Reduviid bug (Triatoma species), also known as the "kissing bug."
  • Diagnostic feature: Romana's sign (unilateral painless periorbital swelling) is a hallmark sign of acute Chagas’ disease, resulting from the site of entry of the parasite.
  • Life cycle forms: The parasite has trypomastigote (found in the blood) and amastigote (found intracellularly in tissues such as cardiac muscle) forms.
  • Culture medium: The parasite can be cultured in NNN (Novy-MacNeal-Nicolle) medium, used for culturing Leishmania and Trypanosoma species.

 

Why Tsetse Fly is Incorrect:

 

The Tsetse fly (Glossina palpalis) is the vector for African sleeping sickness (caused by Trypanosoma brucei, not Trypanosoma cruzi). Chagas’ disease is caused by Trypanosoma cruzi, and the vector is the Reduviid bug.

 

Other Options:

 

Option A. Romana’s sign is a diagnostic feature of acute Chagas’ disease: This is true. Romana's sign is a characteristic swelling at the site of the bite, usually seen around the eye, indicating acute infection.

 

Option C. Cultured in NNN medium: This is true. NNN medium is used to grow both Trypanosoma cruzi and Leishmania.

 

Option D. Has amastigote and trypomastigote forms: This is true. Trypanosoma cruzi exists in both amastigote (intracellular form) and trypomastigote (circulating form) stages in humans.

 

Educational Objective:

 

The vector for Chagas’ disease (Trypanosoma cruzi) is the Reduviid bug (kissing bug), not the Tsetse fly. The Tsetse fly is the vector for African sleeping sickness caused by Trypanosoma brucei.

questions.stem: Neil Mosser reaction or tunica reaction is useful to differentiate between:
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. A) R. prowazekii and R. typhi

 

The Neil-Mooser reaction (also known as the tunica reaction) is used to differentiate between Rickettsia prowazekii (causes epidemic typhus) and Rickettsia typhi (causes endemic typhus).

 

  • Procedure:
    • A male guinea pig is used because of the presence of scrotal tunica.
    • The patient's sample suspected of containing Rickettsia species is injected into the scrotum.
    • If the infection is due to R. typhi (endemic typhus), the scrotum becomes swollen and stony hard due to inflammation within 1-2 days (positive reaction).
    • If the infection is due to R. prowazekii (epidemic typhus), there is no swelling of the scrotum (negative reaction).

 

This reaction works because R. typhi tends to produce more localized inflammation than R. prowazekii.

 

Other Options:

 

Option B. R. typhi and R. rickettsia: R. rickettsia causes Rocky Mountain spotted fever, which presents with a very different clinical syndrome and does not require the Neil-Mooser reaction for differentiation.

 

Option C. R. prowazekii and R. rickettsia: The clinical presentations of epidemic typhus (from R. prowazekii) and Rocky Mountain spotted fever (from R. rickettsia) are distinct, and the Neil-Mooser reaction is not used for this purpose.

 

Option D. R. rickettsia and C. burnetti: Coxiella burnetii causes Q fever, which is unrelated to Rickettsia species and does not require a Neil-Mooser test for differentiation.

 

Educational Objective:

 

The Neil-Mooser reaction is used to differentiate epidemic typhus caused by R. prowazekii (negative reaction) from endemic typhus caused by R. typhi (positive scrotal swelling).

questions.stem: All of the following interaction occurs between antigen antibody reaction except:
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. B) Covalent bond

 

The binding of an antigen to an antibody involves multiple types of non-covalent interactions to ensure specificity and reversibility. 

 

These include:

 

  1. Ionic bonds (electrostatic forces): Attraction between positively and negatively charged regions of the antigen and antibody.
  2. Hydrogen bonds: Bonds formed due to sharing of hydrogen atoms between the antigen and antibody.
  3. Van der Waals forces: Weak, short-range forces caused by the transient dipole moment in atoms.
  4. Hydrophobic interactions: When non-polar regions of the antigen and antibody come together to minimize contact with water.

 

 

  • Covalent bonds are strong, permanent bonds that involve the sharing of electron pairs between atoms. In antigen-antibody interactions, we require transient and reversible interactions to allow the immune system to adapt to changing antigens and avoid prolonged or permanent attachment. Therefore, covalent bonds are not involved in antigen-antibody binding.

 

Educational Objective:

 

Antigen-antibody interactions involve non-covalent bonds such as ionic bonds, hydrogen bonds, Van der Waals forces, and hydrophobic interactions. Covalent bonds do not form in these reactions due to their strong, irreversible nature.




ore, covalent bonds are not involved in antigen-antibody binding. Educational Objective: Antigen-antibody interactions involve non-covalent bonds such as ionic bonds, hydrogen bonds, Van der Waals forces, and hydrophobic interactions. Covalent bonds do not form in these reactions due to their strong, irreversible nature.

questions.stem: Resistance to HIV infection occurs due to mutation of:
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. A) CCR 5

 

HIV infection requires binding of the virus to CD4 receptors and co-receptors on the host cell for successful entry and fusion.

 

  • Primary binding: The gp120 glycoprotein of HIV binds to the CD4 receptor present on CD4 T lymphocytes and macrophages.
  • Co-receptor binding: After primary binding, the viral gp41 glycoprotein interacts with either:
    • CCR5 (chemokine receptor 5)—expressed mainly on macrophages and early stages of infection ("R5 tropic").
    • CXCR4—expressed on T lymphocytes and typically involved in late-stage infection ("X4 tropic").

 

 

CCR5 Mutation:

 

  • In some individuals, especially in populations of European and Western Asian descent, there is a mutation called CCR5-Δ32.
  • This mutation results in the absence of functional CCR5 receptors on the cell surface.
  • Without the CCR5 co-receptor, HIV cannot complete the fusion process, preventing the virus from entering the host cell.
  • These individuals may remain asymptomatic and resistant to HIV infection even after exposure.

 

This mutation offers natural resistance to HIV-1 infection, specifically the R5-tropic virus. However, it does not protect against strains of HIV that use CXCR4 as a co-receptor.

 

Other Options:

 

Option B. CXCR4: CXCR4 is the co-receptor involved in late-stage HIV infections (T-tropic strains). Mutation in this receptor does not confer resistance to the R5-tropic HIV strain.

 

Option C. gp41: gp41 is a glycoprotein of the virus responsible for fusion after attachment. Mutations in host genes (not viral genes like gp41) confer resistance to HIV.

 

Option D. CD4: CD4 is the primary receptor on T lymphocytes and macrophages. Mutations in CD4 are not known to provide resistance to HIV infection.

 

Educational Objective:

 

A mutation in CCR5 (called CCR5-Δ32) confers resistance to HIV infection by blocking the co-receptor binding and fusion step, preventing viral entry into the host cells.

questions.stem: True regarding H. influenzae growth:

options.label: A
options.text: Growth in MacConkey and blood agar but not chocolate agar

options.label: B
options.text: Growth in MacConkey and chocolate agar but not blood agar

options.label: C
options.text: Growth in blood and chocolate agar but not MacConkey medium

options.label: D
options.text: Growth in MacConkey, blood and chocolate agar

questions.answerText: Growth in blood and chocolate agar but not MacConkey medium
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. C) Growth in blood and chocolate agar but not MacConkey medium

 

Haemophilus influenzae is a fastidious organism, meaning it has specific growth requirements. It requires both factor V (NAD) and factor X (heme) for growth:

 

  • Blood agar: Contains factor X (heme) but lacks free factor V, as factor V is trapped within the intact RBCs. Thus, H. influenzae shows scant or no growth on plain blood agar.

 

 

  • Chocolate agar: Made by heating blood agar, which causes the lysis of RBCs, releasing both factor V and factor X into the medium. Hence, H. influenzae grows abundantly on chocolate agar.

 

 

  • MacConkey agar: A selective and differential medium for Gram-negative enteric bacteria. H. influenzae does not grow on MacConkey agar as it is not an enteric bacterium.

 

Satellitism:

 

  • When Staphylococcus aureus is streaked on blood agar, it releases factor V (NAD) as it grows. H. influenzae can grow in the vicinity of S. aureus colonies due to the availability of both factor V and X. This appearance of "satellite" colonies near the S. aureus streak is called satellitism.

 

 

Other Options:

 

Option A. Growth in MacConkey and blood agar but not chocolate agar: Incorrect, as H. influenzae does not grow on MacConkey agar           and shows poor or no growth on plain blood agar.

 

Option B. Growth in MacConkey and chocolate agar but not blood agar: Incorrect, as H. influenzae does not grow on MacConkey agar but shows good growth on chocolate agar.

 

Option D. Growth in MacConkey, blood, and chocolate agar: Incorrect, as H. influenzae does not grow on MacConkey agar, shows poor growth on blood agar, and grows well on chocolate agar.

 

Educational Objective:

 

Haemophilus influenzae requires factor V (NAD) and factor X (heme) for growth. It grows well on chocolate agar (where RBCs are lysed) but does not grow on MacConkey agar. Satellitism can be observed on blood agar when grown near Staphylococcus aureus due to the release of factor V.

questions.stem: Swarming is seen in:
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. A) Clostridium tetani

 

Swarming is a characteristic growth pattern seen on solid culture media, where bacteria spread outwards in a concentric, wave-like manner. This phenomenon occurs due to the bacteria’s motility.

 

Key organisms that exhibit swarming:

 

  • Proteus mirabilis and Proteus vulgaris (commonly associated with swarming on blood agar).
  • Clostridium tetani (anaerobic bacterium known for its "swarmer" cells due to its motility).
  • Bacillus cereus (known for its motile forms).

 

Among the Clostridium species:

 

  • Clostridium tetani (causative agent of tetanus) shows swarming growth due to its highly motile flagellated cells.
  • Clostridium perfringens, botulinum, and difficile do not show swarming as they are either non-motile or minimally motile.

 

Other Options:

 

Option B. Clostridium perfringens: This species does not exhibit swarming. Instead, it grows rapidly with large, opaque colonies on blood agar and shows a double zone of hemolysis.

 

Option C. Clostridium botulinum: Non-swarming and grows as distinct colonies.

 

Option D. Clostridium difficile: Does not swarm but forms flat, irregular colonies with a "horse-stable" odor due to its fermentation products.

 

Educational Objective:

 

Swarming motility is observed in Clostridium tetani, Proteus species, and Bacillus cereus. It is caused by their highly motile nature due to flagella.

questions.stem: A patient admitted to an ICU is on central venous line for the last one week. He is on ceftazidime and amikacin. After 7 days of antibiotics, he develops a spike of fever and his blood culture is positive for gram positive cocci in chains, which are catalase negative. Following this, vancomycin was started but the culture remained positive for the same organism even after 2 weeks of therapy. The most likely organism causing infection is:
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. C) Enterococcus faecalis

 

The scenario indicates a hospital-acquired infection (HAI) in a patient with prolonged ICU stay, central venous line, and multi-drug-resistant infection. The key points in the question:

 

  • Gram-positive cocci in chains: Suggests streptococci or enterococci (as staphylococci appear in clusters).
  • Catalase negative: Rules out staphylococci (since staphylococci are catalase positive).
  • Resistance to vancomycin: Suggests vancomycin-resistant Enterococcus (VRE), which is common in ICU settings due to its multi-drug-resistant nature.

 

Enterococcus faecalis and Enterococcus faecium are commonly associated with nosocomial infections, especially bloodstream infections, in patients with prolonged hospital stays and antibiotic exposure.

 

Other Options:

 

Option A. Staphylococcus aureus: S. aureus appears as gram-positive cocci in clusters and is catalase positive. The case describes catalase-negative cocci in chains, ruling out staphylococci.

 

Option B. Viridans streptococci: While viridans group streptococci can cause endocarditis, they are usually sensitive to vancomycin. They are not typically associated with multi-drug resistance in ICU settings.

 

Option D. Coagulase-negative Staphylococcus: Coagulase-negative staphylococci (CoNS), such as Staphylococcus epidermidis, are catalase positive and grow in clusters, not chains. Hence, they do not fit the description.

 

Educational Objective:

 

Enterococcus faecalis and Enterococcus faecium are gamma-hemolytic streptococci (non-hemolytic) that form catalase-negative chains and are frequently responsible for hospital-acquired infections (HAIs) that are resistant to multiple antibiotics, including vancomycin.

questions.stem: A 15-year-old girl had splenomegaly, leucopenia, step ladder pattern fever and died in a few days. Longitudinal ulcers were found in intestine. What should be the probable diagnosis?
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. A) Typhoid

 

Typhoid fever is caused by Salmonella typhi and is characterized by the following key features:

 

  • Step-ladder pattern fever: The fever rises progressively and plateaus over time, showing a characteristic "step-ladder" pattern.
  • Splenomegaly and leukopenia: Enlargement of the spleen and a decrease in white blood cells are classic findings in typhoid due to the systemic infection.
  • Intestinal findings:
    • Typhoid causes longitudinal ulcers in Peyer's patches of the ileum due to necrosis.
    • The ulcers are longitudinal (lengthwise) along the axis of the intestine.
    • These ulcers can lead to complications such as intestinal perforation or hemorrhage.

 

 

Other Options:

 

Option B. Tuberculosis: Intestinal tuberculosis can cause ulcers, but the ulcers are typically transverse (cross-sectional) to the axis of the intestine. Also, intestinal TB presents more insidiously with abdominal pain, weight loss, and chronic symptoms rather than the acute presentation described in this case.

 

 

Option C. Amebiasis: Amoebic ulcers in the intestine are typically flask-shaped and located in the colon rather than the ileum. Amebiasis presents with dysentery rather than step-ladder fever.

 

Option D. Shigella: Shigella causes bacillary dysentery with bloody diarrhea and superficial ulcers in the colon rather than the ileum. There is no characteristic step-ladder fever in Shigella infections.

 

Educational Objective:

 

Step-ladder pattern fever and longitudinal ulcers in the ileum are classic hallmarks of typhoid fever. Intestinal TB has transverse ulcers, and amebiasis and bacillary dysentery affect the colon, not the small intestine.
